In older adults, the decision to treat with CPAP should be based on symptoms, quality of life, and a comprehensive geriatric assessment (frailty, cognition, autonomy, patient preferences) rather than on OSA severity alone, as this treatment primarily improves symptoms and quality of life, while its cardiovascular benefits and impact on mortality remain uncertain.

papers.title: Electrophysiological properties of mesodiencephalic junction neurons projecting to the inferior olive.
papers.abstract: The neocortex has the largest volume, whereas the cerebellum houses the most neurons of the mammalian brain, underscoring paramount functions for interactions between them. Neocortical projections to the cerebellum involve both the mossy fibre and climbing fibre systems; mossy fibres find their origin predominantly in the pons, whereas the climbing fibres are relayed via subnuclei of the inferior olive (IO) that receive cortical input via the mesodiencephalic junction (MDJ). Given that climbing fibres regulate cerebellar plasticity in a timing-dependent manner, the MDJ-IO pathway probably contributes to both sensorimotor and cognitive learning. However, the physiological properties of IO-projecting MDJ neurons remain largely unknown. Here, we made targeted whole-cell recordings in brain slices of the mouse MDJ, separating IO- from non-IO-projecting neurons following retrograde tracing. We show that IO-projecting neurons are, unlike non-IO-projecting neurons, highly spontaneously active and capable of high-frequency bursts of ≤350 Hz during current injections. Optogenetic stimulation shows that excitatory neocortical inputs to IO-projecting MDJ neurons can be integrated directly with excitatory inputs from the cerebellar nuclei. Moreover, unlike non-IO-projecting neurons, IO-projecting MDJ neurons depolarize and repolarize quickly, and hyperpolarizing inputs consistently trigger rebound action potentials upon stimulus offset. This hyperpolarization is probably induced predominantly by inhibitory inputs from the ventral tegmental area and periaqueductal grey, which provide prominent bilateral inputs to MDJ neurons, as revealed by viral tracing in Gad2-Cre mice. Our results highlight how neocortical inputs to the MDJ can be transformed into diverse IO firing patterns and thereby contribute to the required specifics of cerebellar learning. KEY POINTS: The mesodiencephalic junction is an important brainstem region connecting the cerebral cortex with the cerebellum through its projection to the inferior olive, the sole source of the climbing fibres that drive cerebellar learning. We find that mesodiencephalic junction neurons projecting to the inferior olive represent a population of physiologically distinct neurons, capable of high firing frequencies and rebound activity following hyperpolarization. We reveal that mesodiencephalic junction neurons receive prominent excitatory inputs from neocortex and cerebellar nuclei, whereas their main inhibitory inputs are derived from the ventral tegmental area and periaqueductal grey. These findings shed light on how the activity of neurons in the mesodiencephalic junction can be regulated and how these neurons might influence activity in the inferior olive, and thereby cerebellar learning.

papers.title: Professional Identity, Psychological Resilience, and Adaptive Performance in Junior Nurses Exposed to Workplace Bullying: A Latent Profile and Network Analysis.
papers.abstract: To identify resource-adaptation profiles and profile-specific network organization among junior nurses exposed to workplace bullying by examining professional identity (PID), psychological resilience (PSR), and adaptive performance (ADP). A multicenter, cross-sectional study. Survey data were collected from 7231 junior nurses in 90 tertiary hospitals in Sichuan Province, China; 5839 met the workplace bullying exposure criterion and were included. Latent profile analysis was performed using 36 item-level indicators of PID, PSR, and ADP. Ordered logistic regression examined factors associated with profile membership, and network analysis compared profile-specific resource organization. Robustness was assessed using network comparison tests, residualized networks, hospital-cluster robust sensitivity analysis, and bootstrap stability analyses. Three profiles were identified: the resource-constrained adaptive profile (n = 1906, 32.64%), moderate resource-adaptation profile (n = 3152, 53.98%), and high resource-adaptation profile (n = 781, 13.38%). More frequent night shifts, longer weekly working hours, poorer sleep quality, and lack of regular exercise were associated with greater odds of membership in a more resource-constrained profile. The high resource-adaptation profile showed the highest global network strength (16.223) and the largest mean absolute nonzero edge weight (0.086), despite fewer nonzero edges. PID2 (Social confidence), PID8 (Social interaction), PSR2 (Achievement pride), and PSR3 (Calm handling) repeatedly served as bridge nodes. Bootstrap analyses supported centrality stability, with CS coefficients of 0.750 across base and residualized networks. Junior nurses exposed to workplace bullying showed heterogeneous resource configurations and profile-specific network organization. Integrating latent profile and network analyses showed how PID, PSR, and ADP may be configured and interconnected under a resource-threatening work context.

papers.title: AAV-mediated Modulation of Dorsal Raphe Serotonergic Neurons Recapitulates Fenfluramine Efficacy in a Rat Model of Dravet Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Dravet Syndrome (DS) is a catastrophic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) primarily caused by SCN1A haploinsufficiency. It is characterized by refractory hyperthermia-induced seizures, neurodevelopmental delay, and an elevated risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) compared to other childhood epilepsies. While the small molecule fenfluramine (FFA) provides profound clinical benefit, its potential for systemic side effects and a poorly defined mechanism of action (MOA) underscores the need for more targeted interventions. Using a Scn1a+/- rat model of DS, we demonstrate that chronic FFA treatment reduces the frequency of hyperthermia-induced seizures and attenuates pathological EEG network hypersynchrony. Furthermore, FFA administration ameliorates hyperactivity and depressive-like comorbidities, an effect associated with a marked reduction in hippocampal neuroinflammation and microglial overactivation. Transcriptomic analysis implicated serotonergic signaling in the therapeutic response to FFA, and subsequent anatomical and functional analyses revealed enhanced activity of dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) serotonergic neurons following FFA treatment. Cell-type-specific AAV-mediated modulation of DRN serotonergic neurons was sufficient to reproduce the key antiseizure and electrophysiological effects of FFA. Together, our findings identify the DRN serotonergic circuit as a therapeutically relevant circuit and provide proof-of-concept for mechanism-driven, circuit-specific neuromodulation strategies for Dravet syndrome.
papers.journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy

papers.title: Gel-Free Capture of Microvolt-Level Neural Signatures Via a 3D Monolithic Carbon Fiber Dry Electrode.
papers.abstract: Gel-based wet electrodes remain the gold standard for electrophysiology, but gel dehydration limits recordings. Existing dry electrodes partially address this limitation but suffer from high interfacial impedance. Here, a carbon fiber-based porous electrode (CFPE) is reported, comprising a three-dimensional conductive network coated with poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrene sulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS). The CFPE establishes contact at hairy-scalp sites with an impedance of approximately 10 kΩ·cm2. On the forearm, its impedance at 10 Hz without skin preparation is 11.09 ± 1.03 kΩ·cm2, compared with 13.57 ± 2.07 kΩ·cm2 for wet electrodes. After 6 h of wear, CFPE impedance reaches 1.3 times its initial value without skin preparation or gel, whereas wet-electrode impedance reaches 56 times its initial value when applied with skin preparation and conductive gel. High-fidelity electrocardiography, electromyography, and electroencephalography signals are captured with correlation coefficients exceeding 90% and signal-to-noise ratios comparable to wet electrodes. The CFPE further resolves microvolt-level speech-evoked frequency-following responses (FFR) and long-latency responses (LLR), with fidelity comparable to wet electrodes and significantly higher LLR SNR. These results demonstrate gel-free acquisition of weak neural biomarkers, opening a pathway toward prolonged, preparation-free neurophysiology.

papers.title: Deciphering the molecular basis of maize cold tolerance via integrative regulatory network analysis.
papers.abstract: Maize (Zea mays L.) is a globally critical but cold-sensitive crop. Understanding the temporal organization of cold-responsive, circadian-associated, and hormone-associated transcriptional programs is essential for deciphering how plants balance growth and survival under cold stress to ensure food security. We performed high-resolution time-series RNA-seq on 108 maize seedling samples across 14 time points (0-36 h cold stress and 24 h recovery). Coronatine (COR) was utilized as a defined JA-associated chemical perturbation to probe hormone-associated transcriptional responses during cold stress. We identified 12 986 cold-responsive and 2259 recovery-responsive genes, revealing a recovery-associated transcriptional transition characterized by suppressed photosynthesis-related processes and enrichment of genes associated with lipid catabolism, accompanied by transient physiological stress during early recovery. Cold stress induced widespread phase shifts and reduced oscillation amplitudes among circadian-associated transcripts, while COR identified distinct hormone-associated transcriptional modules and candidate network-associated genes, including ZmWRKY71 and ZmHSP28, whose roles were further supported by molecular and genetic analyses. This study establishes a temporally resolved transcriptional framework for maize cold stress and recovery, integrating transcriptional dynamics, physiological responses, and experimentally supported regulatory nodes.
papers.journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology

papers.title: Mediating Roles of Sleep Disturbances and Depressive Symptoms in the Association Between Chronic Pain and Cognitive Dysfunction in Older Adults.
papers.abstract: To identify the associations between chronic pain and cognitive dysfunction and the mediating roles of sleep disturbances and depressive symptoms among older adults. Eight electronic databases were searched for studies reporting pairwise correlation coefficients among chronic pain, sleep disturbances, depressive symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction in older adults. Two reviewers independently conducted study screening, data extraction, and quality assessment. Two-stage structural equation modeling was applied to integrate correlation evidence across studies and estimate direct, indirect, and serial pathways. Thirty-eight studies involving 34,126 older adults were included. The pooled correlation matrices showed significant correlations between chronic pain and cognitive dysfunction, sleep disturbances, and depressive symptoms. TSSEM further identified a significant direct association between chronic pain and cognitive dysfunction, as well as significant indirect pathways through depressive symptoms and through the serial pathway involving sleep disturbances and depressive symptoms. Chronic pain, sleep disturbances, depressive symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction were interrelated in older adults. These findings support a focused biopsychosocial interpretation of the association between chronic pain and cognitive dysfunction.

papers.title: Clinician-guided digital CBT-I improves sleep quality and apnea severity in patients with co-morbid insomnia and OSA: A Double-Blind, Randomized Clinical Trial.
papers.abstract: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the accepted first-line treatment for insomnia, but its scalability and safety in patients with co-morbid insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea (COMISA) remain unclear. Clinician-guided digital CBT-I (D-CBT-I) is a potential treatment option that may address these limitations in COMISA. To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician-guided D-CBT-I versus sleep hygiene education (SHE) in patients with COMISA. This randomized trial (n = 88) compared clinician-guided D-CBT-I (6 weekly online sessions: sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relapse prevention) with SHE alone. Blinded outcome assessments were conducted at baseline, posttreatment (6 weeks), and 3-month follow-up. Primary outcomes were Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores at posttreatment and 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes included daytime sleepiness, sleep parameters, OSA severity, neurocognitive function, and adverse events. At 3-month follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis showed significantly greater improvements with D-CBT-I versus SHE on ISI (-9.5 vs. -4.0 points; d = -1.18, P = 0.001) and PSQI (-4.9 vs. -1.8 points; d = -0.87, P = 0.001); D-CBT-I also reduced subjective sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale; -3.4 vs. -1.0 points; d = -0.68, P < 0.001). At posttreatment, D-CBT-I reduced the apnea-hypopnea index (attended in-laboratory polysomnography; -6.0 vs. +2.0 events/h; d = -0.64, P = 0.019). Although transient increases in ESS occurred at weeks 2-4, no functional impairment or sleepiness-related adverse events were reported. Additional benefits were observed in metacognition and executive function. Clinician-guided D-CBT-I improved insomnia and OSA severity, and enhanced cognitive function in COMISA patients. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry; NO.: ChiCTR2500099854; URL: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=267457.
papers.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

papers.title: Seasonal Variation in Mood and Associated Patterns of Sleep, Activity, Circadian Rhythms and Light.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms underlying seasonal mood variation are incompletely characterised. We tested whether wearable-measured sleep, activity, circadian and light exposure patterns are associated with seasonal mood variation in young Australians with emerging mood disorders. We analysed 733 observation periods from 422 participants (mean age 24.3 ± 5.5 years; 63% female) attending early-intervention clinics. Each observation included a clinical assessment paired with ≥5 valid days of wrist actigraphy. Season was modelled using sine-cosine functions of day-of-year. Sleep, activity and circadian features were reduced using joint and individual variation explained (JIVE). Light exposure features were reduced using principal component analysis (PCA) applied to light regularity, timing and exposure interval across 7 illuminance thresholds. Linear mixed-effects models tested seasonal effects on clinical outcomes; indirect associations for 12 candidate JIVE/PCA variables were estimated by cluster bootstrap. Depressive symptoms (β = -0.67, P = .023) and negative symptoms (β = -0.17, P = .041) peaked in winter, whereas manic symptoms peaked in autumn (β = 0.24, P = .019). Winter increases in negative symptoms were associated with an 'extended sleep with phase-delayed activity' profile (indirect β = -0.015, P < .002) and a 'constrained pattern of moderate-to-bright indoor light exposure' profile (indirect β = -0.038, P = .002), reflecting high day-to-day consistency with a narrow daily exposure window. The light association persisted after adjustment for time spent above the light threshold, which itself was not associated with symptoms. Winter increases in depressive symptoms were associated with lower overall physical activity levels (indirect β = -0.009, P = .040). No indirect associations were identified for manic symptoms. In this transdiagnostic youth sample, seasonal variation in mood was modest but was accompanied by differences in how personal light exposure was arranged across the day, not only in how much light was received and in daily activity patterns. These cross-sectional associations identify light patterning and activity rhythms as candidate modifiable targets for prospective and interventional research.

papers.title: Bilateral cortical network disruptions in the rat caudal forelimb area after unilateral stroke.
papers.abstract: To investigate how ischemic stroke alters neural activity in the caudal forelimb area (CFA) and identify electrophysiological mechanisms underlying post-stroke motor deficits. Local field potentials were recorded bilaterally from ipsilateral and contralateral CFA in rats under anesthesia and during a single-pellet retrieval task. Analyses included spectral power across canonical frequency bands, aperiodic 1/f slope characterization of excitation-inhibition balance, and cross-frequency coupling assessment of interhemispheric coordination. Stroke induced widespread bilateral disruptions in oscillatory dynamics across delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. The aperiodic 1/f slope shifted, reflecting altered excitation-inhibition balance. Cross-frequency coupling between hemispheres, particularly low-frequency phase to gamma amplitude, was reorganized, indicating impaired interhemispheric coordination and bilateral motor network imbalance. Notably, the main experimental cohort did not include a sham-operated control group; however, a pilot experiment with three sham and three MCAO animals, conducted using identical procedures, provided supportive evidence for the stability of key measures under sham conditions. This study demonstrates that ischemic stroke induces coordinated alterations in spectral organization, excitation-inhibition balance, and cross-frequency interactions within the bilateral caudal forelimb cortex. These findings indicate that post-stroke motor dysfunction arises from disrupted, state-dependent dynamics of distributed motor networks rather than isolated changes within the lesioned hemisphere.

papers.title: Three repeated intrathecal injections of allogenic umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stromal cells in autism spectrum disorder: a Phase I clinical trial.
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition of etiology, characterized by deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors. Despite its growing prevalence, no treatment has yet demonstrated consistent efficacy across the full spectrum of ASD phenotypes. This Phase I, open-label study investigates the safety and feasibility of three repeated intrathecal injections of allogeneic Umbilical Cord Tissue-Derived Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (UC-MSCs) in children diagnosed with ASD. Five children (aged 3-7) with ASD, confirmed by Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders- Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria and on stable behavioral and pharmacologic regimens for at least two months, received three intrathecal (IT) injections of 20 × 10⁶ UC-MSCs at one-month intervals. Safety was monitored over six months based on Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE). Preliminary behavioral assessments, including the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC), and the Behavior Problem Inventory (BPI-S), were conducted at the baseline, one-, two-, four-, and six-month follow-ups. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytokine profiles were measured prior to each injection. Electroencephalography (EEG) and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) were performed at baseline and the final follow-up. The treatment was safe and well-tolerated with no serious adverse events (SAEs). All participants experienced at least one mild to moderate, transient adverse event (AEs), most commonly fever (5/5) and nausea (4/5). Exploratory behavioral improvements were observed in CARS in all children, while two participants moved from the mild-to-moderate to the non-autistic ranges, and three shifted from the severe to the mild-to-moderate range. Other measures also improved, though the persistence of these improvements was varied. CSF cytokines showed consistent reduction, particularly in TNF-[Formula: see text] and IL-6 levels across participants, confirming the immunomodulatory impact of UC-MSC administration. The EEG findings revealed that the spectral pattern shifted toward a more typical profile in one participant after treatment. This Phase I study showed that three repeated IT injections of UC-MSCs are safe and well-tolerated in children with ASD. Preliminary behavioral and biomarker improvements warrant further study in larger controlled trials. Trial Registration ID: IRCT20200217046526N3.

papers.title: Improvement in naming with tDCS and alteration of functional connectivity in post-stroke aphasia: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effects of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (A-tDCS) over the left Sylvian parietal temporal region (SPT) on picture naming and auditory comprehension, as well as changes in brain functional connectivity in post-stroke aphasic patients. This is a double-blind, sham-controlled, randomized controlled study. Sixty aphasic patients were randomly assigned to receive either active or sham tDCS over the SPT as well as speech-language therapy for four weeks. Standardized aphasia assessments and electroencephalogram (EEG) examinations were conducted before and after the treatment. The EEG nonlinear index of cross approximate entropy (C-ApEn) was used to assess brain functional connectivity. The tDCS group demonstrated significantly greater improvements than the control group in both picture naming and auditory word-picture identification scores (p < 0.001). Regression analysis revealed that the group (tDCS/control) was the primary factor associated with improving picture naming. The functional connectivity of F3-P3, F7-P3, T3-T5, T5-P3, T5-C3, T4-T6, T3-T4, and T5-T6 significantly increased following tDCS. Anodal tDCS over the left SPT can improve picture naming and auditory comprehension in subacute post-stroke aphasia. Potential mechanisms include enhanced connectivity within the left-hemisphere dorsal/ventral streams, the executive control network, and between the bilateral temporal lobes. These functional connectivity changes provide neural evidence for the effect of tDCS on naming improvement. Clinical trial registry number ChiCTR-TRC-14005072.

papers.title: Predictors of academic self-efficacy in medical intern students: the roles of mindful eating, physical activity, sleep quality, and mental workload.
papers.abstract: Academic self-efficacy, defined as an individual's belief in their capacity to complete academic tasks, may play a role in the learning and performance of medical students. Lifestyle factors such as sleep quality, physical activity, and mindfulness-based behaviors have been associated with cognitive performance and psychological well-being and can influence academic self-efficacy. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the associations between these factors and academic self-efficacy among medical interns. This cross-sectional study included 165 medical interns (53.3% male, mean age 25.83 ± 1.65 years) from Shiraz University of Medical Sciences who completed validated questionnaires assessing mindful eating, mental workload, academic self-efficacy, sleep quality, and physical activity. Multiple regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors. The mean academic self-efficacy score was 3.32 ± 0.52 out of 5 points. Significant predictors of overall academic self-efficacy included the following: mindful eating subscales (awareness: β = 0.16, p = 0.046; disinhibition: β = 0.195, p = 0.018; external cues: β = 0.275, p = 0.003), physical activity (β = 0.13, p = 0.039), sleep quality (sleep latency: β = -0.27, p = 0.002; sleep efficiency: β = -0.195, p = 0.026; subjective sleep quality: β = -0.22, p = 0.005), and mental workload (physical demand: β = -0.185, p = 0.027; temporal demand: β = -0.195, p = 0.025). The full model explained 41.5% of the variance in academic self-efficacy. Similar patterns were observed across all four subscales. Higher academic self-efficacy in medical interns was significantly associated with more mindful eating, higher physical activity, better sleep quality, and lower mental workload. These findings suggest that future research should evaluate multidimensional interventions targeting these modifiable factors to increase medical students' academic self-efficacy.

papers.title: General information reliability, perceived educational quality, and transparency of YouTube videos on epileptiform discharges: an exploratory cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is central to diagnosing and classifying epileptiform discharges, but interpretation requires structured training. This exploratory cross-sectional study evaluated general information reliability and completeness, perceived educational quality, and transparency of English-language YouTube videos on epileptiform discharges. Although these patterns are described using established electrographic criteria, interpretation may vary, particularly in borderline recordings. A cross-sectional YouTube search was conducted in May 2025 using five keywords. The first 100 results per keyword were screened and 25 of 500 records met all eligibility criteria. The final sample was limited to narrated, English-language videos lasting 1 to 20 min that were returned by the selected search terms and YouTube ranking system. Two neurologists independently rated the videos using DISCERN as a general reliability indicator, the Global Quality Scale (GQS) for educational quality, and the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) criteria for transparency. Exploratory analyses included group comparisons, Spearman correlations, single-measure intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), effect sizes, confidence intervals, and false-discovery-rate-adjusted q values. Six videos (24%) were from academic/educational channels and 19 (76%) from individual healthcare professionals. Mean scores were 52.1 for DISCERN (95% CI 46.7-57.5), 3.86 for GQS (95% CI 3.58-4.14), and 1.98 for JAMA (95% CI 1.69-2.27). Single-measure ICCs were 0.971, 0.655, and 0.816, respectively. Duration was nominally correlated with GQS (ρ = 0.431, p = 0.031) and JAMA (ρ = 0.553, p = 0.004), and DISCERN with GQS (ρ = 0.496, p = 0.012); none remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction (all q ≥ 0.052). Among the small subset of eligible videos, general-purpose instruments suggested moderate-to-good average perceived educational quality and information reliability, whereas transparency was limited. Because DISCERN, GQS, and JAMA are not EEG-specific and no qualitative EEG-accuracy, pedagogical, or learner-outcome assessment was performed, the findings are exploratory. These results should not be understood as estimating the quality of all YouTube material related to EEG or epileptiform discharges, nor do they establish EEG-specific accuracy or educational effectiveness. The evaluated videos should therefore be used only as critically appraised adjuncts to expert-supervised EEG training.

papers.title: The journey of numbers from attention to motor processing: an embodied account of neural response to number magnitudes.
papers.abstract: Embodied cognition suggests numbers are linked to physical actions and sensory experiences. Additionally, sensory processing, thoughts or actions are modulated by attentional shifts/control. This study investigates how learned motor associations in individuals (finger-counting habits) shape brain responses to digit symbols. We examined how covert attention to motor associations influences neural responses during passive viewing of symbolic numbers, using event-related potentials (ERPs) and time-frequency analysis. We examined whether the P2 component, linked to attentional processing, correlates with motor habits and alpha wave activity. Results showed stronger P2 component when number-hand associations aligned, with no significant alpha wave changes was observed. Right-starters exhibited enhanced attention and number processing, with higher P3 amplitudes and faster responses for all digits. Taken together, these findings provide preliminary support for the idea that attention to learned motor associations may influence neural responses to numerical information. We discuss these findings within our proposed theoretical framework termed Feature-based Attention to Learned Motor (FALM) processing.

papers.title: Associations of alarm fatigue with occupational burnout and sleep quality in ICU nurses: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Alarm fatigue is a critical concern in intensive care units (ICUs), where nurses are continuously exposed to high volumes of clinical alarms. This phenomenon has been associated with psychological strain, impaired sleep quality, and occupational burnout. Despite growing evidence, limited studies have simultaneously explored the associations among these variables in ICU nurses. This study aimed to investigate the relationships among alarm fatigue, occupational burnout, and sleep quality in ICU nurses working in hospitals in Kerman and Sirjan, Iran. A descriptive-analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 219 ICU nurses selected through census sampling. Data were collected using a demographic questionnaire, the Alarm Fatigue Scale (AFSS), the Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI), and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 22, employing independent t-test, ANOVA, Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman's correlation coefficient, and multivariable linear regression analyses. A significance level of p < 0.05 was considered. More than half of the nurses reported no alarm fatigue (57.5%), while 83.6% experienced poor sleep quality. Emotional exhaustion was low to moderate in most participants, depersonalization was moderate in 56.2%, and reduced personal accomplishment was reported by 96.3%. Alarm fatigue showed weak but statistically significant positive correlations with poor sleep quality (r = 0.230, p = 0.001) and occupational burnout (r = 0.166, p = 0.014). Sleep quality was also weakly but significantly correlated with occupational burnout (r = 0.175, p = 0.010). Alarm fatigue and burnout were significantly associated with gender, employment status, shift type, and general health status. Alarm fatigue, poor sleep quality, and occupational burnout are related occupational health concerns among ICU nurses. Higher alarm fatigue was weakly but significantly associated with poorer sleep quality and greater burnout. These findings suggest that alarm management, shift scheduling, and workforce-related factors may be relevant areas for organizational attention; however, future longitudinal and interventional studies are needed to determine whether such strategies improve sleep quality, reduce burnout, or enhance patient safety. Not applicable.

papers.title: Preserved ovarian reserve in night-active versus day-active women: a cross-sectional comparison of neuroendocrine markers.
papers.abstract: Shift work inverts the sleep-wake cycle and may perturb circadian-controlled reproductive hormones, yet its effect on ovarian reserve in young women is uncertain, and data on the circadian-sensitive neuropeptides kisspeptin and melatonin are scarce. We compared ovarian reserve and serum kisspeptin, melatonin, and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) between night-active and day-active women. In this cross-sectional study, 90 healthy women aged 18-35 years with normal body mass index were enrolled (46 night-active, 44 day-active). On cycle day 3, ovarian reserve was assessed by ultrasonography (ovarian volume, antral follicle count [AFC]) and biochemistry (FSH, LH, estradiol, anti-Müllerian hormone [AMH]); prolactin, TSH, vitamin D, kisspeptin, and melatonin were also measured. Groups were compared with distribution-appropriate tests and covariate-adjusted ANCOVA. Ovarian reserve was similar between groups: ovarian volume (p = 0.623), AFC (median 6.0 vs. 6.0, p = 0.791), and AMH (2.7 vs. 3.1 ng/mL, p = 0.862) did not differ, nor did FSH, LH, estradiol, prolactin, or vitamin D (all p > 0.05). Night-active women had higher median kisspeptin (889.5 vs. 336.2 ng/L, p < 0.001), melatonin (699.9 vs. 225.1 ng/L, p < 0.001), and TSH (2.0 vs. 1.5 mU/L, p = 0.020), and shorter sleep duration. The kisspeptin and melatonin differences persisted after covariate adjustment; the TSH difference did not. The primary effect of a night-active circadian rhythm was neuroendocrine rather than gonadal: ovarian reserve was not detectably altered in young, normal-BMI women, while kisspeptin, melatonin, and TSH were higher. These neuroendocrine differences are hypothesis-generating: because the groups were sampled at opposite points of the daily rhythm (~ 21:00 vs. ~ 09:00), they cannot be separated from a time-of-sampling effect and likely reflect circadian state rather than altered hormone output.

papers.title: The impact of menstruation-related symptoms on women's quality of life, work productivity, and economic burden: a structured narrative review.
papers.abstract: Menstruation-related disorders, including dysmenorrhoea, premenstrual syndrome (PMS)/ premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), and heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB)/ abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), are common among women of reproductive age and associated with impairments in quality of life (QOL), mental health, and daily functioning. Increasing evidence indicates that these conditions adversely affect academic and work productivity, with presenteeism constituting a major component of the economic burden. However, the existing evidence remains fragmented. We conducted a structured narrative review supported by a targeted literature search of PubMed and Scopus. Studies published in English between January 2014 and December 2025 were considered if they included female individuals aged 14-59 years and examined menstruation-related symptoms in relation to QOL, work productivity, academic or occupational functioning, or economic outcomes. Because of heterogeneity in study designs, populations, and outcome measures, findings were synthesised thematically rather than quantitatively pooled. A total of 86 studies were used to inform the thematic synthesis. Across conditions, menstruation-related disorders were consistently associated with reduced health-related QOL, psychological distress, and impaired academic and occupational functioning. Productivity loss was observed across disorders and predominantly driven by presenteeism rather than by absenteeism. Dysmenorrhoea and PMS/PMDD were associated with both absenteeism and presenteeism, whereas HMB/AUB was strongly associated with work impairment, which is frequently mediated by anaemia-related symptoms. Psychological distress, including anxiety, depressive symptoms, emotional dysregulation, and sleep disturbance, has emerged as a key contributor to QOL impairment across age groups and regions. Lifestyle factors appeared to modify symptom severity and functional impact. Although treatment and medical consultations often improved symptoms, productivity gains were inconsistent. This review highlights the multidimensional burden of menstruation-related disorders extending from physical symptoms to mental health and functional outcomes. The predominance of presenteeism suggested that conventional metrics based on absenteeism underestimate the true societal impact. The observed gap between symptom improvement and functional recovery underscored the need for integrated approaches that could address both clinical and psychosocial pathways.

papers.title: Markers of blood-brain barrier and intestinal mucosal barrier in insomnia disorder: an observational study linking wake-promoting neurotransmitters to sleep efficiency.
papers.abstract: The present study aimed to investigate the alterations in wake-promoting neurotransmitters (histamine and orexin-A) and markers of blood-brain barrier and intestinal mucosal barrier including zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1), claudin-5, zonulin, and S100 calcium-binding protein B (S100β) in insomnia disorder (ID). Additionally, we examined the correlations between these neurotransmitters and barrier markers, and explored their combined associations with sleep parameters. This study enrolled 54 ID patients and 45 healthy controls. The demographic and clinical characteristics of all participants were investigated, and participants underwent overnight polysomnography. Serum levels of wake-promoting neurotransmitters and barrier markers were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Spearman's correlation analysis was conducted to explore the associations between these serum biomarkers and sleep parameters, as well as between the neurotransmitters and barrier markers. Furthermore, mediation analysis was performed to examine whether barrier markers mediated the relationship between wake-promoting neurotransmitters and sleep parameters. Levels of peripheral wake-promoting neurotransmitters (histamine and orexin-A) and barrier markers (zonulin, S100β, ZO-1, and claudin-5) were elevated in the ID group (all p < 0.001). Additionally, sleep efficiency was positively correlated with histamine levels (r = 0.57), negatively correlated with orexin-A levels (r = -0.62), and positively correlated with ZO-1 levels (r = 0.56) in ID patients. Moreover, histamine levels showed positive correlations with claudin-5 (r = 0.37) and ZO-1 (r = 0.31), and a negative correlation with S100β (r = -0.33). Additionally, orexin-A was negatively correlated with claudin-5 levels (r = -0.46). Furthermore, ZO-1 showed a statistical mediation effect in the associations between histamine and sleep efficiency (p = 0.006) as well as between orexin-A and sleep efficiency (p = 0.012), consistent with a potential indirect pathway. This study observed dysregulation of peripheral wake-promoting neurotransmitters along with markers of blood-brain barrier and intestinal mucosal barrier in ID patients. Notably, ZO-1 showed a statistical mediation effect in the associations between these neurotransmitters and sleep efficiency, though causality cannot be inferred from the cross-sectional design. These clinical findings provide preliminary insights into the molecular features associated with ID and may inform directions for future mechanistic research. Further studies are needed to fully elucidate the underlying mechanisms.

papers.title: Health4Life: a digital intervention to promote healthy diet and movement behaviours from the start of life: protocol for a hybrid effectiveness-implementation study.
papers.abstract: Globally and in Sweden childhood overweight and obesity remain major public health issues. The first 1000 days (i.e., conception-24 months) has been identified as the period of greatest developmental plasticity, with the maximum capacity to influence health throughout life. As obesity-related behaviours, including excessive screen time and poor dietary habits, have been found to establish in infancy and continue into early childhood, this demonstrates the need for early life health promotion interventions. Therefore, the aim of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of and explore the implementation of a digital intervention (Health4Life app) designed to support parents in creating healthy diet and movement behaviours from the start of their infant's life, to promote health and prevent overweight and obesity. A two-arm parallel open-label randomized controlled trial, using a hybrid type I implementation-effectiveness design will be conducted. Families will be recruited at the 6-week routine visit at participating child health service (CHS) centers (n = 504). If parents' consent to participate families will be randomized in a 1:1 ratio into the control or intervention group. Both groups receive standard care; however, the intervention group also receives access to the 16-month Health4Life app-based intervention. Primary outcomes are children's dietary intake (questionnaire), physical activity and sleep (accelerometry), and screen time (questionnaire). Secondary outcomes are children's body mass index z-scores (measured at CHS) and parental self-efficacy for promoting health behaviours (questionnaire). The implementation outcomes being explored are acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility according to CHS nurses (semi-structured interviews) as well as parental satisfaction and usage of the Health4Life app (questionnaires and semi-structured interviews). An important mission of CHS is to support parents in establishing healthy diet and movement behaviours, and the Health4Life app is designed to support this by providing early and tailored guidance to families. If shown to be effective as well as acceptable, appropriate and feasible, Health4Life has the potential to be implemented as a complement to CHS nurses' routine work to promote children's health and development in accordance with the Swedish national child health monitoring program. This trial was registered at Clinicaltrials.gov (ID NCT06798597) on January 29th, 2025.

papers.title: Sex differences in associations between sleep architecture and CBC-derived immune cell indices in MDD with comorbid insomnia.
papers.abstract: Insomnia symptoms and alterations in sleep architecture are core pathophysiological features of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). While sex differences in MDD prevalence and symptomatology are well documented, the specific interplay between sleep architecture and complete blood count (CBC)-derived immune cell indices, metabolic markers, and thyroid-related parameters remains under-characterized with respect to sex. This study included 126 patients with MDD and comorbid insomnia (43 males, 83 females). All participants underwent overnight polysomnography (PSG) and fasting blood biochemical analysis. Sex-specific associations between objective sleep parameters and peripheral biomarkers were analyzed using age-adjusted partial Spearman correlation and multiple linear regression models with interaction terms. Female patients had longer REM sleep latency and N2 sleep duration, whereas male patients had a higher apnea-hypopnea index. Females had higher HDL-C levels, while males had higher monocyte counts. In age-adjusted FDR-corrected correlation analyses, significant associations involving CBC-derived immune cell counts were observed primarily in male patients, where lymphocyte count was associated with TST, REM sleep duration, N1%, and N2 sleep duration; no significant CBC-derived immune cell count correlations remained in female patients. In multivariable interaction analyses with FDR correction, sex × lymphocyte interaction terms remained significant for TMA, REM sleep duration, and REM sleep duration relative to TST. These findings suggest that sex may shape both the subjective-objective expression of sleep disturbance and lymphocyte-related sleep regulation in patients with MDD and comorbid insomnia. The pattern of poorer subjective sleep quality despite relatively favorable selected PSG characteristics in females, together with sex-dependent lymphocyte associations involving REM sleep and arousal measures, warrants further validation in larger longitudinal studies. Not applicable.

papers.title: Association between lactic dehydrogenase-to-albumin ratio and all-cause mortality in critical obstructive sleep apnea patients: a retrospective cohort study from the MIMIC-IV database.
papers.abstract: Our study endeavors to elucidate the link of the lactic dehydrogenase-to-albumin ratio (LDAR) to all-cause mortality (ACM) among the critically ill obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) population. A retrospective observational cohort study was performed leveraging the MIMIC-IV 3.1 data. This study encompassed adult OSA patients first entering the intensive care unit (ICU). Patients were stratified into quartiles by LDAR. The primary outcomes were ACM at 30, 90, 180 days, and one year after ICU entry. ACM across LDAR quartiles was compared via the Kaplan-Meier (KM) survival analysis. The relation of LDAR to ACM was examined utilizing multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression and restricted cubic spline (RCS) models. The consistency and robustness of our findings were rated through subgroup, interaction, and sensitivity analyses. One thousand one hundred eighteen critically ill OSA patients were encompassed. 749 (66.99%) were male, with a median age of 66. The 30-day, 90-day, 180-day, and one-year ACM rates were 14.58%, 19.59%, 22.00%, and 26.74%. KM curves demonstrated significantly higher mortality rates across increasing LDAR quartiles (log-rank P < 0.001). After possible confounders were adjusted, LDAR was independently related to elevated 90-day ACM risk (HR, 1.318; 95%CI, 1.142-1.520) as a continuous variable. In contrast to the lowest LDAR quartile, the highest quartile displayed a 139.8% greater likelihood of 90-day ACM (HR, 2.398; 95%CI, 1.512-3.803; Ptrend < 0.001). Similar relations were noted for 30-day, 180-day, and one-year ACM. RCS analysis revealed a positive linear relation of LDAR to death at all time points (Pnonlinear > 0.05). Subgroup and interaction analyses revealed insignificant effect modification, confirming the robustness of the association across various clinical strata. Among the critically ill OSA population, elevated LDAR is independently and linearly related to elevated ACM risk in short-term and long-term mortality. The foregoing findings suggest LDAR as a valuable prognostic biomarker for risk classification and clinical management among this high-risk population.

papers.title: Pain characteristics and risk of scale-identified cognitive impairment among middle-aged and older Chinese adults: a longitudinal study from CHARLS.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment and chronic pain have become major public health challenges, adversely affecting the lives of middle-aged and older adults. However, longitudinal evidence on pain characteristics and subsequent cognitive outcomes in Chinese populations remains limited. We examined whether baseline pain characteristics were associated with the risk of developing scale-identified cognitive impairment among middle-aged and older Chinese adults. This longitudinal cohort study included 7,899 CHARLS participants aged 45 years and older who were free of scale-identified cognitive impairment at baseline in 2015 and had follow-up cognitive assessment data in 2020. Pain distribution and location were assessed by self-report. Cognitive function was measured using episodic memory and mental acuity tests, and scale-identified cognitive impairment was defined as a cognitive function score at least 1 SD below the wave-specific mean. Cox regression models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics, lifestyle factors, sleep duration, and number of chronic diseases. Over an average follow-up period of 60.1 months, 21.2% of participants developed scale-identified incident cognitive impairment. Compared with the no-pain group, those experiencing multi-site pain exhibited a modestly higher risk of incident cognitive impairment (adjusted HR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.05 to 1.33). Subgroup analyses revealed that the risk remained significant among females (adjusted HR = 1.26, 95% CI: 1.05 to 1.51) and individuals aged < 60 years (adjusted HR = 1.21, 95% CI: 1.03 to 1.44). Participants with headache-associated pain had a higher risk of scale-identified incident cognitive impairment (adjusted HR = 1.33, 95% CI: 1.15 to 1.53) compared with those without pain. Multi-site pain and headache-associated pain were associated with modestly elevated risks of scale-identified incident cognitive impairment. Considering the scale-identified cognitive outcomes and self-reported pain assessment, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Future studies with more detailed pain measures and longer follow-up are warranted.

papers.title: Association between brain functional state indices and eye movement features in patients with anxiety disorders: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: This study systematically examined the differences in brain functional states and eye movement performance among patients with anxiety disorder and explored their associations using real-world data. A total of 195 patients with anxiety disorders were enrolled between January 2023 and June 2024. Psychological assessments included SAS (Self-Rating Anxiety Scale) and PSQI (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) instruments. Brain functional indices and eye movement parameters (prosaccade task, antisaccade task and smooth-pursuit task) were collected. Group comparisons, correlation analyses, and logistic regression models were employed to evaluate the contributions and predictive performance of these markers. Patients showed significantly lower Brain Inhibition, Stability, and Emptying Indices, and higher Emotion Resistance and Anxiety Tendency Indices. Eye movement tests revealed prolonged latencies and completion times in prosaccade and antisaccade tasks. Significant correlations were observed between brain functional state indices and eye movement performance. The eye-movement-based model yielded a higher area under the curve (AUC) (0.895) than the brain-function-based model (AUC = 0.621). Combined brain functional and eye movement indices may serve as objective, adjunctive measures for the assessment of anxiety disorders, reflecting underlying neural dysregulation. Not applicable.

papers.title: Network analysis of frailty, sleep quality, and life satisfaction in older patients: a cross-sectional study stratified by chronic disease burden.
papers.abstract: Multimorbidity and chronic disease burden are common among older patients and are closely associated with frailty, poor sleep, and reduced subjective well-being. However, total-score-based analyses may obscure item-level interactions across health domains. This study examined the network structure of frailty, sleep quality, and life satisfaction in older patients and explored whether association patterns varied across chronic disease burden levels. This cross-sectional study included 1,107 older patients. Multimorbidity was defined as the presence of two or more chronic diseases. Frailty, sleep quality, and life satisfaction were assessed using the Fatigue, Resistance, Ambulation, Illnesses, and Loss of Weight (FRAIL) scale, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), respectively. A regularized partial correlation network was estimated using the graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) with extended Bayesian information criterion (EBIC) model selection (EBICglasso), with scale items or components as nodes. Strength, expected influence, and bridge centrality were calculated. Stratified analyses were conducted by number of chronic diseases, and bootstrap procedures were used to assess network accuracy and stability. Multimorbidity was present in 1,078 participants (97.4%), and the median number of chronic diseases was 5 (IQR, 3-6). Network analysis showed that SWLS-related nodes had relatively high strength and bridge strength, indicating relatively high statistical connectivity within the overall network and across communities. Sleep-related nodes, particularly sleep latency, use of sleeping medication, and daytime dysfunction, were prominent in signed centrality indices. Frailty nodes were mainly connected to SWLS nodes through negative edges. The SWLS community showed dense internal connections, whereas frailty and sleep quality were linked to life satisfaction primarily through negative cross-community edges. In descriptive stratified analyses, negative cross-community connections appeared more pronounced in the group with ≥ 5 chronic diseases. Because the cutoff was data-driven and no formal network comparison test was performed, the apparent between-group differences should be interpreted as descriptive and exploratory rather than statistically confirmed. Network stability analyses indicated acceptable stability. Among older patients, life satisfaction-related nodes showed relatively high overall connectivity, while several sleep-related nodes showed notable statistical associations within the estimated network. Given the high prevalence of multimorbidity in this sample, multidisciplinary assessment and health management should consider the interrelations among sleep problems, frailty, and life satisfaction in the context of chronic disease burden. Network analysis may provide exploratory evidence on cross-domain associations in complex health problems among older patients, but apparent differences across chronic disease burden groups require confirmation using formal network comparison tests and longitudinal designs.

papers.title: Prevalence and characteristics of headache among medical students in Abidjan: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Headache disorders are among the most common neurological complaints worldwide, particularly among medical students who are exposed to high academic stress. This study aimed to assess the prevalence and clinical characteristics of headaches among medical students in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire. A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted from February to May 2025 among 506 medical students at Félix Houphouët-Boigny University in Abidjan (response rate: 25.0%). Data were collected using a self-administered online questionnaire (Google Forms), which included sections on sociodemographic characteristics, headache frequency and duration, headache types classified according to ICHD-3 criteria, triggering factors, and associated symptoms. Multiple responses were allowed for triggering factors. Among the 506 participants, 269 (53.2%) were female, with a mean age of 22 years (range: 16-33 years). Headaches were reported by 493 students (97.4%). Tension-type headaches were the most frequent (55.0%), followed by migraine (30.0%) and secondary headaches (15.0%). The distribution of headache phenotypes differed significantly according to sex (χ² = 21.9, df = 2, p < 0.001). Secondary headaches were mainly self-reported as related to dental, sinus, ENT disorders, or malaria. Tension-type headaches were predominantly bilateral (52.6%), whereas migraine was more often unilateral (33.7%). The mean frequency of headache episodes was 3.46 per month and 9.56 over six months, indicating a mostly episodic course. The main triggering factors included lack of sleep (91.5%), prolonged screen exposure (52.4%), and stress (50.6%). Multiple responses were allowed for triggering factors. Headaches are highly prevalent among medical students in Abidjan, predominantly tension-type. Lifestyle and academic-related stress are major contributors, highlighting the need for preventive strategies and health education in university settings.
papers.journal: The journal of headache and pain

papers.title: How Patients with Atopic Dermatitis Experience Topical Therapy: A Real-World Analysis of Impact, Treatment Satisfaction, and HCP Communication.
papers.abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic, burdensome skin condition with significant impact on quality of life. Topical therapies are recommended as first-line treatment; however, patients with moderate-to-severe disease or inadequate disease control may require escalation to systemic therapy. Despite the central role of topical therapies in AD management, real-world data on treatment satisfaction and healthcare provider (HCP)-patient concordance remain limited. This analysis draws on data from the Adelphi Real World Atopic Dermatitis Topical Plus Wave I Disease Specific Programme (DSP)™, a cross-sectional, real-world survey conducted in 2025 among 267 US adolescents and adults with current moderate-to-severe AD. Using linked surveys, we evaluated treatment satisfaction and communication dynamics between HCPs and patients/caregivers using topical therapies, both with and without advanced systemic therapy. Kappa analysis assessed HCP-patient/caregiver agreement. At time of survey completion, 233 participants had moderate AD (87%), as assessed by a HCP, with 34 participants (13%) having severe AD. Participants in both the topical medication only (TM) (n = 193; 72%) and topical plus advanced systemic therapy (TAS) (n = 74; 28%) groups reported day-to-day impacts on clothing choices, daily activities, and sleep. Notably, 68% of patients using topical therapies reported disliking how their topical therapy made their skin feel, underscoring a persistent daily treatment burden. Regarding satisfaction, moderate concordance between patient/caregiver and HCP ratings was observed among individuals receiving TM (κ = 0.57; p < 0.001) and those with moderate AD (κ = 0.46; p < 0.001), with fair concordance among patients/caregivers receiving TAS (κ = 0.27; p = 0.001) and those with severe AD (κ = 0.25; p = 0.031). Communication analysis revealed moderate concordance between HCPs and patients/caregivers with respect to instructions for application amount (TM: κ = 0.54, p < 0.001; TAS κ = 0.42, p < 0.001). These findings highlight persistent gaps in satisfaction and communication for patients with moderate-to-severe AD prescribed topical medications, underscoring the need for individualized treatment approaches. Addressing these gaps may help address unmet needs and inform more individualized care.

papers.title: A systematic review of economic evaluations of strategies to diagnose obstructive sleep apnoea in adults.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a chronic condition characterised by recurrent episodes of apnoea and hypopnoea. People with untreated OSA are at increased risk of excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), functional impairment and developing cardiovascular conditions, metabolic and neurocognitive diseases. EDS is a key determinant of quality of life (QoL) and is associated with increased healthcare utilisation and accident risk. Untreated OSA can also lead to impaired work productivity, reduced health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and life expectancy, which contribute to the UK economic burden. To review and critically appraise all published economic evaluations that assessed the cost-effectiveness of devices and strategies to diagnose and manage people with moderate-to-severe OSA. This systematic review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews guidelines and registered in the Prospective Register of Ongoing Systematic Reviews (CRD42024535732). We searched electronic databases up to March 2025. Two reviewers undertook screening, data extraction and quality appraisal using recognised reporting quality and methodological quality appraisal tools. The findings were summarised and discussed narratively. Twenty-nine studies were included. Fifteen studies included an economic evaluation alongside a clinical trial and 14 studies were model-based economic analyses. Although many analyses were methodologically sound in their overall approach, there were concerns regarding choice of time horizon, selection of health states, undertaking pre-model analyses and long-term adherence and efficacy of continuous positive airway pressure treatment (CPAP). Substantial methodological heterogeneity was identified across studies, including variation in diagnostic thresholds and scoring criteria used, model structures and assumptions regarding treatment adherence. Only four of twenty-nine included studies used home respiratory polygraphy (HRP) as a comparator, limiting the direct applicability of much of the evidence to the UK setting. Past economic analyses offer insight into the methods used to assess the cost-effectiveness of strategies to diagnose OSA. These economic analyses are a useful framework to build on, but clear gaps exist in the clinical and economic evidence. Future economic evaluations should prioritise contemporary diagnostic pathways and technologies, use consistent diagnostic definitions, and incorporate more realistic modelling of long-term treatment adherence and benefit. Until such information becomes available, the true cost-effectiveness of these strategies remains unknown.

papers.title: Glymphatic Dysfunction as a Multisystem Pathway Linking Systemic Health Conditions to Alzheimer's Disease: Mechanisms, Risk Factors, and Therapeutic Opportunities.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system is a glia-associated perivascular pathway involved in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-interstitial fluid (ISF) exchange and the transport and clearance of neurotoxic metabolites, including amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau, from the central nervous system. Growing evidence suggests that alterations in glymphatic and perivascular clearance are associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology and may contribute to the accumulation of neurotoxic proteins and neurodegeneration. This review examines the role of the glymphatic system in AD and explores how aging, sleep disturbances, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, high-fat diet, diabetes, and gut microbiome dysbiosis impair glymphatic transport. A recurring mechanism across experimental models is the loss of perivascular AQP4 polarization, while vascular, metabolic, and inflammatory conditions may converge on related perivascular and neurovascular processes that impair CSF-ISF exchange and solute handling. Neuroimaging studies using markers such as DTI-ALPS, perivascular space burden, and free-water measurements provide evidence of alterations in glymphatic-related and perivascular processes in AD and demonstrate associations with amyloid deposition, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline. Furthermore, glymphatic dysfunction may interact with neuroinflammation and tau pathology, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that accelerates disease progression. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including continuous theta-burst stimulation, positive airway pressure therapy for obstructive sleep apnea, pharmacological enhancement of AQP4 function, and nutritional interventions, have shown potential in experimental and early translational studies to influence glymphatic-related processes and may mitigate AD-related pathology. Collectively, current findings suggest that glymphatic and perivascular clearance pathways may represent an important link between systemic health conditions and AD. Because related pathways are implicated across multiple systemic conditions, interventions targeting glymphatic and perivascular dysfunction may have broader relevance to brain health, but their clinical effects remain to be established.

papers.title: Antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri induce ribosomal condensation to inhibit translation.
papers.abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a global health threat requiring antimicrobials with alternative modes of action. Growing evidence indicates that bacteria organize key intracellular processes through biomolecular condensates and other forms of spatial organization, yet whether such spatial organization can be exploited as an antimicrobial target remains unclear. Here, we identify intrinsically disordered antimicrobial peptides, generated from the Drosophila sleep-inducing protein Nemuri, that inhibit bacterial growth by targeting ribosomal organization. Mechanistically, these peptides enter bacterial cells without overt membrane disruption and accumulate in ribosome-rich regions, where they bind broadly to RNA and ribosomal surfaces through multivalent interactions. This engagement remodels ribosome-rich regions into condensates with reduced ribosomal mobility, thereby suppressing global protein synthesis and distinguishing these peptides from canonical site-specific ribosome-targeting antibiotics. Furthermore, Nemuri-derived peptides exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, including activity against drug-resistant pathogens, with low cytotoxicity toward Drosophila and mammalian cells. Together, our findings identify the organization and material dynamics of bacterial ribosomes as a biophysical vulnerability that can be exploited by antimicrobial peptides, revealing how a naturally evolved metazoan host-defense system turns intracellular organization itself into an antibacterial target.

papers.title: Amygdala beta bursts modulate hippocampal neuronal dynamics during human emotional processing.
papers.abstract: The amygdala and hippocampus are key structures in emotional processing, yet the transient neural dynamics coordinating their interaction remain poorly understood. We simultaneously recorded single-neuron activity and local field potentials from these regions in epilepsy patients performing an emotional image-rating task. Neurons in both regions exhibited firing rate changes predictive of subjective emotional valence. While conventional spectral analysis revealed no valence-specific patterns, beta bursts (13-30 Hz)-transient, high-power events-were selectively modified by task features. In both regions, beta bursts were associated with increased gamma amplitude and enhanced phase coherence, with beta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling capturing emotion-related dynamics. Critically, amygdala beta bursts were associated with valence-dependent, bidirectional modulation of hippocampal interneuron firing - decreased during very unpleasant/highest arousal processing and increased during high-arousal very pleasant processing - while putative pyramidal-cell firing did not change significantly. Hippocampal bursts showed no reciprocal influence. These findings suggest that beta bursts may represent a temporally precise neural correlate of emotional appraisal and a potential target for neuromodulation in mood disorders.

papers.title: Clock neurons modulate seizure timing through a diurnal switch.
papers.abstract: People with epilepsy experience daily oscillations in seizure risk. Using a video-tracking model to automate detection, we explored mechanisms underlying spontaneous seizures in Drosophila and find that flies, like people, exhibit daily oscillations in seizure risk. These rhythms are absent in flies lacking a molecular circadian clock and are independent of sleep. Thermogenetic screening and cell-specific clock perturbations reveal that the ventrolateral neurons, including "morning cells", and dorsolateral neurons, comprising the "evening cells", modulate diurnal oscillations in seizure risk. Pigment-dispersing factor and short neuropeptide F from morning cells increase seizure risk during the day. During this time, morning cell activity increases whole-brain activity. At night, morning cells switch to glycine signaling likely acting on evening cells to decrease seizure risk. Optogenetic inhibition of clock neurons suppresses seizure risk. Our findings reveal an unexpected role for brain clock neurons in modulating daily seizure risk.

papers.title: Outcomes of a randomized-controlled digital weight management program over 2.5-years.
papers.abstract: Coaching-led digital weight-loss interventions are successful in the short-term, but have limited evidence supporting long-term changes. This study evaluated a commercially available behavioral weight-management program compared to digital control on initial and long-term outcomes. A total of 684 participants were screened to achieve a sample of English-speaking individuals 18-60 years old with a body mass index (BMI; kg/m2) > 27 kg/m2 without contraindications to using a smartphone program. In a single-blinded, parallel-group trial, a centralized computer-generated program randomized 600 participants (n = 302 intervention; n = 298 control) to a 6-month intervention or control with a maintenance phase during months 7-30. The primary outcome was change in BMI; secondary outcomes included effects on diet, physical activity, sleep, quality of life, psychosocial functioning, and health status. Fifty-seven participants withdrew from the study and all future assessments; 78% of the sample completed 6-months and 65% completed 30-month follow-up. All available data were used under assumptions of missing at random. Latent growth curve models showed the differences were not significant [β = 0.99, 95%CI = -1.38, 3.36, d = .17, 95%CI = -0.24, 0.58]. Over 30-months, changes for intervention and control were 0.13 kg/m2 (SD=3.09) and 0.58 kg/m2 (SD=3.64), respectively, a significant difference [β = -4.42, 95%CI = -8.72, -0.12, d = -0.76, 95%CI = -1.51, -0.02]. Although the acute effects on self-reported BMI were not significant, the use of coaching-led weight loss led to better two-year BMI outcomes, and were greater for those at a lower BMI. Interventions using personal support may be important for realizing longer-term benefits of digital interventions.

papers.title: Comment on "Living in a shared room is associated with worse pain and sleep during hospital admission after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair".

papers.title: Daytime Sleepiness, Insomnia Symptoms and Sleep Quality in Adults Entering a Structured Weight-Loss Programme: The SCOOP-RNPC Cohort.
papers.abstract: Daytime sleepiness, insomnia and poor sleep quality are common in adults with overweight/obesity. This study characterized these sleep-related complaints and their associations with clinical characteristics at entry into the Nutritional and Psycho-Behavioural Rehabilitation (RNPC) programme, identified clinical characteristics associated with impaired sleep health, and explored changes after weight loss. This observational study was conducted within the prospective SCOOP-RNPC cohort. Adults with overweight/obesity completed the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) questionnaires. An exploratory questionnaire-based summary score (0-6) was used to describe combined sleep-related profiles and compare baseline clinical characteristics. Longitudinal changes were explored in participants with assessments at baseline and programme end. Of 1886 participants with complete baseline sleep questionnaire data, 20.2% reported excessive daytime sleepiness (ESS score > 10), 23.4% had moderate-to-severe insomnia symptoms (ISI ≥ 15) and 63.3% reported poor sleep quality (PSQI > 5). For the exploratory summary score, 22.7%, 50.3% and 27.0% of participants had scores of 0-1, 2-4 and 5-6, respectively. In those with longitudinal data (n = 310), changes in sleep-related questionnaire scores were observed during follow-up, and the proportion with a summary score of 5-6 increased from 31.0% to 45.5%. Sleep-related issues were common among adults entering structured weight-loss care. Less favourable questionnaire-based sleep profiles were associated with a greater burden of subjective symptoms. In exploratory longitudinal analyses, improvements in sleep-related questionnaire outcomes were observed during the weight-loss phase, although interpretation is limited by selective follow-up and the absence of a control group.

papers.title: Circadian clock adjusted classes improve sleep, circadian health, and academic performance in medical freshmen.
papers.abstract: University students often experience circadian misalignment with academic schedules, which may impair performance. This study evaluated whether a later-start schedule improves academic outcomes and circadian rhythms in first-year medical students. Incoming students (n = 220) completed the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire; those with high social jetlag (SJL >120 min, n = 71) were randomized into either a later-start schedule (LS; classes ≥10:00 a.m., n = 30) or a standard early-start schedule (ES; 8:00 a.m., n = 41). Actigraphy data were collected from 112 students prior to examinations. Based on the objective temperature circadian phase (TCP) with a median acrophase split at 3:59 a.m. ES participants were categorized asearly (ETCP-ES, n = 41) or late (LTCP-ES, n = 41). All LS participants exhibited a TCP later than 3:59 a.m. and remained LTCP-LS group (n = 30). Associations between scheduling, circadian metrics, and exam scores were analyzed using regression and sex-adjusted ANCOVA. TCP predicted exam scores overall (β = -0.217, p = 0.021), most evidently within ES (β = -0.291, p = 0.008). LTCP-ES students scored lower than ETCP-ES students (p = 0.025). LTCP-LS students performed similarly to ETCP-ES students and showed greater circadian robustness, including higher rest-activity stability (p = 0.031), greater blue-light stability (p = 0.029), and longer sleep duration (p = 0.013).

papers.title: State-Dependent Modulation of Corticospinal and Cortical Responses by Closed-Loop Paired-pulse TMS.
papers.abstract: Brain oscillations shape cortical excitability in a phase-dependent manner. Cortical excitability reflects the net output of intracortical circuits, including inhibitory and facilitatory pathways. However, whether the phase of ongoing brain rhythms differentially modulates inhibitory and facilitatory responses remains unknown. Paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (ppTMS) can selectively engage these circuits, providing a unique tool to dissociate their contributions. We combined real-time EEG-guided closed-loop TMS with single- and paired-pulse TMS in 24 healthy adults (13 female) to probe how sensorimotor mu (8-13 Hz) and beta (14-30 Hz) oscillatory phase shapes responses associated with intracortical inhibitory and facilitatory processes. Single-pulse TMS (spTMS), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) were delivered at four phases (peak, falling, trough, rising). Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) and TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs) were recorded to assess corticospinal and cortical responses, respectively. We found that MEP amplitude was phase-dependent across all three stimulation types, with spTMS-evoked and ICF-conditioned MEPs showing the largest amplitudes at the rising phase, whereas SICI-conditioned MEPs were largest at the peak phase of the mu oscillation. TEP P60-N100 amplitude was modulated by oscillatory phase across all stimulation types, with maximal responses at the trough phase. SICI showed opposing phase patterns between the two measures, revealing a dissociation between cortical and corticospinal responses. MEP and TEP preferred phases were correlated across participants only in the ICF condition. These findings extend phase-dependent spTMS effects to paired-pulse stimulation and show that ongoing mu phase differentially shapes responses to SICI and ICF across cortical and corticospinal levels.Significance Statement Ongoing brain oscillations are known to shape cortical excitability across their phase cycle. However, whether this effect differentially influences inhibitory and facilitatory responses has remained unresolved. Here, using closed-loop EEG-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation in healthy adults, we probed how SICI- and ICF-conditioned responses vary across different phases of the sensorimotor mu and beta rhythms. We show that corticospinal and cortical responses to inhibitory and facilitatory paired-pulse protocols exhibit distinct phase-dependent patterns in the sensorimotor mu rhythm. These findings extend phase-dependent stimulation effects beyond single-pulse TMS and reveal that the relationship between cortical state and stimulation response differs across paired-pulse protocols.
