The method was tested for nine bolt-ons: breathing, cognition, hearing, self-confidence, skin irritation, sleep, social relationships, tiredness, and vision. We used general-population samples from 14 countries, with 10,395-42,206 observations per bolt-on, and patient samples from six disease areas, with 312-2,486 observations. Core-dimension disutilities were based on the UK EQ-5D-5L value set, and bolt-on disutilities were taken from published studies. Associations of the contraction parameter with bolt-on disutilities and core-dimension correlations were assessed using linear regression. Achieving consistency required contraction factors ranging from 0.871 for breathing to 0.989 for sleep. Stronger contraction was required for bolt-ons with larger disutilities and for those more strongly correlated with the core dimensions, although only the former association was statistically significant. The contraction method aligns EQ-5D-5L+bolt-on value sets with EQ-5D-5L value sets, reducing potential double counting while preserving the increased sensitivity provided by bolt-ons.
papers.journal: The European journal of health economics : HEPAC : health economics in prevention and care

papers.title: Predicting in-silico ventricular tachycardia induction on fuzzy cardiac digital twins.
papers.abstract: Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death (SCD). To date, clinical VT risk assessment is either inaccurate, invasive or expensive. Patient-specific computer modeling of heart electrophysiology (EP) is a promising non-invasive risk assessment approach. It has three major limitations: computational cost, inaccurate arrhythmogenic substrate geometry and unknown patient-specific tissue EP properties. We present a pacing outcome predictor (POP) that quickly identifies the conditions needed to induce VT in three-dimensional personalized cardiac computer models. The POP is used to test VT induction across multiple model versions of a patient, covering scar geometry and EP property variations, with an added layer of model reduction to further accelerate calculations. The results are combined into a personalized VT risk metric based on in-silico VT inducibility across the patient's models. In a retrospective 10-patient repaired Tetralogy of Fallot cohort, the metric showed complete separation (10/10) between patients with and without clinically inducible VT, suggesting potential for non-invasive VT risk assessment in this population.

papers.title: Early ERP processing of self-referential language processing in voluntary and involuntary action contexts: N170 and EPN.
papers.abstract: Understanding how the brain differentiates self from others through language represents an important topic in psychology, linguistics, and social cognition. Within an embodied cognition framework, the present EEG study investigated early neural responses to isolated German pronouns varying in self-relatedness (self-, other-, and self/other-related) and grammatical type (personal vs. possessive). Forty right-handed native German speakers silently read visually presented pronouns while EEG activity was recorded. Two task contexts were employed, involving voluntary and involuntary keypress responses following stimulus presentation. Event-related potential (ERP) analyses revealed significant modulations of the N170 and Early Posterior Negativity (EPN) components. N170 amplitudes varied as a function of pronoun type and self-relatedness, with self-related and other-related pronouns eliciting different responses from ambiguous second-person forms. EPN amplitudes differed across self-reference categories, with additional interactions involving hemisphere and pronoun type. Together, these findings suggest that even minimal linguistic stimuli such as pronouns engage early neural processes sensitive to self-relatedness and linguistic context. Task conditions also differed in early ERP amplitudes; because responses in the immediate-response condition overlapped the ERP measurement intervals, these differences are reported without functional attribution.

papers.title: Participation in an integrated telemedicine and psychological counseling program and psychological outcomes in patients with HCC: a multicenter retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: To examine associations between cumulative participation in an integrated telemedicine and psychological counseling program and psychological outcomes in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). This retrospective cohort included 349 patients at two Chinese hospitals during 2022-2023. Recorded cumulative completion defined low (< 50%), moderate (50-79%), and high (≥ 80%) participation. Twelve-month ANCOVA included 331 patients without recorded death, 50 imputations for nondeath missing outcomes, and 16-17 covariates and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 18 contrasts. The service-recorded WHOQOL-BREF aggregate was exploratory because its scoring algorithm could not be verified. Progression-specific pattern-mixture analyses assessed missingness assumptions. Compared with low participation, moderate and high participation were associated with lower PHQ-9 scores (β = - 2.64; 95% CI - 3.36 to - 1.92 and - 3.73; - 4.49 to - 2.98, respectively), lower PSQI (β = - 1.99 and - 1.09) and distress scores (- 0.53 and - 0.87), and higher exploratory WHOQOL-BREF aggregates (4.69 and 3.45); all q < 0.05. High participation was also associated with lower GAD-7 (- 1.14; - 1.84 to - 0.43). Direct high-moderate comparisons favored high participation for depression and anxiety and moderate participation for sleep. FACT-Hep scores were lower with both moderate (- 8.70; - 11.68 to - 5.73) and high participation (- 8.93; - 12.31 to - 5.55). Participation showed outcome-specific associations, with more favorable psychological scores alongside poorer disease-specific quality of life. Clinical significance remains uncertain. Selection, residual confounding, cumulative exposure timing, and informative attrition limit interpretation; the findings do not establish an optimal participation level.
papers.journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer

papers.title: Chronic Intermittent Hypoxia Aggravates the Pyroptosis of Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells Through Regulating Mitophagy-Mediated NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)-induced renal injury is triggered by chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH). Our previous article has revealed that CIH triggers the pyroptosis of renal tubular epithelial cells through the activation of NLRP3 inflammasome, whereas the mechanism by which CIH activates NLRP3 inflammasome remains elusive. Rats and HK-2 cells were exposed to CIH to establish CIH models. Histopathological staining, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine (Scr) levels were examined to assess renal injury. Western blot and immunofluorescence assay were used to assess proteins related to NLRP3 inflammasome, pyroptosis and mitophagy. Mitochondrial membrane potential and production of ROS and ATP were examined to evaluate mitochondrial function. CCK-8, LDH release and ELISA assays were performed to assess cell injury and inflammation. Mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi-1) was applied for a rescue assay. CIH induced renal injury and suppressed mitophagy in vivo, evidenced by worsening pathological features, elevated Scr and BUN levels, reduced colocalization of Tom20 with LC3B, and downregulated expression of LC3-II/I ratio, Atg5, PINK1 and Parkin. PINK1 overexpression restored mitophagy by enhancing colocalization of mitochondria with LC3B, upregulating LC3-II/I ratio and Atg5, and restored mitochondrial function of CIH-exposed HK-2 cells through enhancing mitochondrial membrane potential, reducing ROS production and increasing ATP content. PINK1 overexpression alleviated cell viability, inflammation and NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis in CIH-exposed HK-2 cells, which were partly abolished by Mdivi-1. PINK1 attenuated NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis in CIH-exposed HK-2 cells partially through restoring mitophagy and mitochondrial function, providing potential therapeutic strategies for OSA-related kidney diseases.
papers.journal: Journal of biochemical and molecular toxicology

papers.title: Psychometric validation of the Ru-SATED 4.0 multidimensional sleep health scale in a representative U.S. sample.
papers.abstract: To develop and psychometrically validate a self-report questionnaire assessing multidimensional sleep health among U.S. adults using item response theory (IRT) and classic test theory analyses. The Ru-SATED 4.0 scale evaluates 6 sleep health dimensions (Regularity, Satisfaction, Alertness, Timing, Efficiency, Duration). We assessed the scale's comprehensibility with cognitive interviews (n=23) and Lexile analysis. We administered Ru-SATED and other self-reported measures to an adult sample (N=2,000; 18-89y) from the YouGov.com Internet panel, representative of the U.S. population in terms of age, sex, race/ethnicity, and education. We used factor analysis to identify the best combination of 6 items (1 per dimension); calibrated these using IRT Graded Response Models; and examined associations with validated measures to establish construct validity. Cognitive interviews confirmed comprehensibility of the items and response options. The final 6 items had excellent model fit in factor analysis (RMSEA=0.08, SRMR=0.03, CFI=0.97, TLI=0.95). IRT calibration showed individual items varied in their degree of severity assessed (location parameters) and amount of information contributed (discrimination parameters) to overall test scores (θ values). Ru-SATED scores demonstrated moderate internal consistency (r=0.7), convergent validity with other sleep scales (|r|=0.3-0.6), and test-retest reliability (r=0.6) one month later. Ru-SATED scores had smaller correlations with depression/anxiety measures (|r|=0.3-0.4), indicating discriminant validity, and differed significantly among individuals with and without self-reported sleep disorders (Cohen's d=0.93, 95% CI=-1.04-0.81). To our knowledge, this is the first study of Ru-SATED scores using IRT and classic test theory analyses. Ru-SATED 4.0 is a psychometrically-valid self-report scale to measure multidimensional sleep health.

papers.title: CMD-Net: A Hybrid CNN-Mamba Denoising Network for NMR Spectroscopy.
papers.abstract: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is essential for chemical and biological analysis, yet its inherent insensitivity frequently yields noise-corrupted spectra that complicate weak signal detection and quantitative measurements. Here, we propose CMD-Net, a hybrid CNN-Mamba denoising network, to recover clean NMR signals closely approximating the high-SNR reference spectrum acquired with a large number of scans. The architecture integrates CNN-based local feature extraction with Mamba-2 global context modeling within a U-shaped encoder-decoder framework, enabling direct noise reduction in the frequency domain. Trained solely on synthetic 1D NMR data, CMD-Net can be applied to 1D heteronuclear spectra and 2D/3D NMR data sets. Extensive validation demonstrates that CMD-Net consistently outperforms state-of-the-art denoising methods across multiple noise levels, achieving superior weak peak preservation and artifact suppression. With a balance between performance and model size, CMD-Net holds promise for low-SNR spectral analysis and protein structural studies in chemistry, biology, materials science, and life science.
papers.journal: The journal of physical chemistry letters

papers.title: Anxiety and Adult ADHD Symptoms Among Occupational Injury Cases Presenting to the Emergency Department: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Work-related injuries have economic and psychosocial consequences. Emerging evidence suggests neurocognitive and affective factors, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms and anxiety, may contribute to occupational injury risk; however, data integrating these factors in emergency department (ED) settings remain limited. This study aimed to compare ADHD and anxiety symptom burden between adults with occupational injuries and age- and sex-matched non-injured controls and to evaluate symptom associations with occupational injury. Adults presenting to a tertiary ED in Türkiye with occupational injuries and age- and sex-matched non-injured controls were assessed using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) and Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI). Sociodemographic, occupational, hazard, injury, and clinical variables were recorded. Logistic regression evaluated factors independently associated with occupational injury, and correlations with sleep duration were analyzed. A total of 609 participants were included (292 injured; 317 controls). Injured workers showed higher ASRS and BAI scores than controls (p < .05). ASRS and BAI scores demonstrated gradients across occupational hazard class, trauma mechanism, and clinical outcomes, including hospitalization and impairment. Prior injury history was more frequent among injured workers. In multivariable analysis, occupational hazard class, ASRS scores, and BAI scores remained independently associated with occupational injury. Sleep duration showed moderate negative correlations with ASRS and BAI scores. Adult ADHD and anxiety symptoms were associated with occupational injury in ED presentations. Screening for neurocognitive and affective vulnerabilities, together with fatigue and sleep management strategies, may enhance occupational injury prevention efforts. Further longitudinal studies are warranted.

papers.title: Adaptive Compared With Persistent Fatigue in Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation Survivors.
papers.abstract: Clearly demarcating the differences between adaptive fatigue, a normal physiological phenomenon, and persistent fatigue, a symptom that requires treatment, is vital for phenotypic characterization in allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (alloHCT) survivors. This study compared the phenotypic characteristics (symptoms and behavioral manifestations) of alloHCT survivors with adaptive versus persistent fatigue using 2 approaches to categorize fatigue. This 2-group, comparative study examined differences in sleep, emotional distress, cognitive functioning, and pain in 38 alloHCT survivors with adaptive compared with persistent fatigue using 2 approaches to classify fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale cut scores and responses to standard clinical questions regarding occurrence, duration, and resolution of fatigue with rest). More alloHCT survivors were classified as having persistent fatigue (n = 27, 71%) using the Fatigue Severity Scale compared with the standard clinical questions (n = 17, 45%). AlloHCT survivors with persistent fatigue reported significantly greater emotional distress and reduced cognitive abilities compared to those with adaptive fatigue when using the Fatigue Severity Scale. No significant differences were found between the 2 groups using standard clinical questions. Persistent fatigue is empirically different from adaptive fatigue. The phenotypic characteristics differed depending on the classification method (cut scores on the Fatigue Severity Score or responses to standard clinical questions). Understanding how methods to classify fatigue influenced the results is important to avoid under- or overtreatment of persistent fatigue and the co-occurring symptoms and behavioral manifestations. Recognizing and identifying therapeutic targets for persistent fatigue is essential for delivering comprehensive survivorship care in alloHCT survivors.

papers.title: Gene-by-Sleep Duration Interaction for Glycemic Traits in More Than 480,000 Individuals.
papers.abstract: The biological mechanisms of how sleep duration impacts type 2 diabetes pathogenesis and glycemic control are unclear. This study reveals 16 loci (11 novel) that interact with either short or long sleep duration to influence hemoglobin A1c, fasting glucose, or fasting insulin. Short and long sleep duration loci were nonoverlapping. Regulation of copper and diacylglycerol levels appear as distinct cellular mechanisms implicated by long and short sleep duration loci, respectively. Identified gene targets present insight for potential type 2 diabetes therapeutic design approaches related to JIP1-c-Jun N-terminal kinase interaction disruption, pericyte health, N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor activity, anti-inflammatory and leptin-enhancing dietary supplements, and serpins.

papers.title: Predictors of Lower Back Musculoskeletal Disability Among Emergency Department Healthcare Professionals: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs), particularly lower back (LB) pain are highly prevalent in emergency department (ED) healthcare professionals with significant health-related impacts due to the high and unexpected workload. This study aimed to identify the predictors of LB disability among ED healthcare professionals in Jordan, including physical, psychological, and ergonomic occupational factors. A multicenter convenience sample of ED healthcare professionals was recruited from Jordanian ED departments. Data collection included demographics, ergonomics-related factors and a group of validated outcome measures: the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS-21). A stepwise multivariable linear regression model was used to identify predictors of LB disability. The study included 447 participants, of whom 57% were male (n = 255) and had a mean age of 35.1 ± 7.0 years. Predictors of the ODI (R2 = .31) included depression (B = 0.456, p < .001), taking sick leave in the past 12 months (β = 6.8, p < .001), safe handling and posturing practices (B = -5.584, p < .001), age (B = 0.32, p < .001) and presence of musculoskeletal injury in the past 12 months (B = 4.6, p = .022). This study highlights the burden of LB disability among ED healthcare professionals. LB disability was significantly associated with depression, recent Musculoskeletal injury, Musculoskeletal-related sick leave and older age, with safe handling and posture practices showing a protective effect. Comprehensive interventions to integrate ergonomic improvements, mental health support, workload optimization, and exercise programs.

papers.title: Impact of Social Vulnerability on Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the association between the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and pediatric obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) outcomes, including comorbidities, diagnostic timing, and surgical intervention. A retrospective review of our institution's TriNetX Research Enterprise Data Warehouse assessed patients aged 0-18 years diagnosed with OSA from 2014 to 2024. Patients were grouped into four SVI quartiles: Low, Low-Medium, Medium-High, and High. Extracted variables included polysomnography (PSG), Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP), tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy (T&A) surgeries, secondary complications, and the time elapsed between diagnosis and procedures or complications. The study included 5753 patients with an average age of 7.69 years, and 43.9% were in the High SVI quartile. Black or African American patients comprised 75.9% of this highly vulnerable cohort. Overall, 8.7% of the cohort underwent PSG, with no significant differences in testing or time to PSG. There was a significant stepwise increase in comorbid asthma across vulnerability tiers, peaking at 9.4% in the High SVI group (p = 0.001). High SVI patients underwent T&A at significantly higher rates compared to those in the Low (p = 0.008) and Low-Medium (p = 0.002) quartiles. The mean time to surgery was 166.5 days, which did not significantly differ between SVI groups. Children in highly vulnerable neighborhoods experienced a disproportionate burden of comorbid asthma and underwent surgical management for OSA at significantly higher rates. This suggests that socially vulnerable patients may present with more severe disease requiring surgery. Incorporating metrics like SVI into clinical pathways can better guide patient-centered care and equitable resource allocation.

papers.title: Lower and earlier diurnal cortisol signatures of psychological trauma versus comparable physiological stress: one day post-exposure.
papers.abstract: Traumatic events engage stress physiology, with the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and cortisol central to adaptation. In naturalistic trauma, physical injury and psychological distress often co-occur, complicating interpretation of acute cortisol changes. Stillbirth offers a natural contrast: it is physiologically similar to live birth but constitutes traumatic bereavement. This study tested whether psychological trauma elicited by stillbirth is associated with acute alterations in diurnal cortisol rhythm versus comparable physiological delivery stress. Fifty-seven postpartum women were included (stillbirth, 24; live birth, 33). Saliva samples were collected at seven fixed time points across the day following childbirth. Cosinor curve fitting yielded the midline estimating statistic of rhythm, amplitude, and acrophase. Traditional indices included area under the curve with respect to ground, area under the curve with respect to increase, and the cortisol awakening response. Group differences were tested using analyzes of variance. Both groups showed a coherent diurnal pattern. Compared with live birth, stillbirth was associated with a lower area under the curve with respect to ground, a lower area under the curve with respect to increase, and a lower midline estimating statistic of rhythm. Stillbirth was also exhibited associated with an earlier acrophase. Compared with comparable physiological delivery stress, stillbirth is linked to reduced total cortisol secretion, lower mean levels, and an advanced circadian phase in the acute postpartum period, suggesting that the psychological trauma of stillbirth may involve alterations in hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis regulatory patterns and providing preliminary evidence for future work on early biological markers and supportive interventions.

papers.title: Levodopa and Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation Modulate Excitation/Inhibition Balance and the Neural Encoding of Isochronous Sequences in Persons With Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Temporally regular auditory stimuli, as found in isochronous sound streams, metronome beats, or music, are often used in rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) interventions to initiate and stabilize the temporal coordination of motor plans in persons with Parkinson's disease (pwPD). Research suggests that RAS promotes the recruitment of a cerebellar-prefrontal network and recalibrates abnormal β-band synchronization in the striato-thalamo-cortical pathway. These cuing effects can resemble those observed via dopaminergic treatments (e.g., levodopa) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the subthalamic nucleus (STN). Here, we investigated the influence of both levodopa administration and STN DBS on the neural encoding of isochronous auditory sequences in pwPD. A comprehensive analysis of electroencephalography (EEG) data revealed changes in β-band event-locked neural responses, as well as event-related potentials, neural tracking of rhythm (δ-band inter-trial phase coherence), and excitation/inhibition balance (E/I) as a function of these treatments. Furthermore, we characterized the link between changes in E/I and motor symptom severity (UPDRS-III) with levodopa administration. We suggest that characterizing individual responses to specific treatments is a fundamental step in tailoring rehabilitation protocols and optimizing intervention efficacy.
papers.journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Real-Time Electronic Patient-Reported Outcome Monitoring With Digital Triage and Care-Team Integration in Early Breast Cancer: ENABLE Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Electronic patient-reported outcomes (ePROs) can support patient-centered oncology care, but in early breast cancer, it is unclear whether real-time ePRO-triggered triage adds benefit beyond lower-intensity app-based support and scheduled ePRO collection. We tested whether adding weekly ePRO screening, rule-based triage, and care-team escalation to app-based support improves health-related quality of life (HRQoL) during systemic therapy for early breast cancer. ENABLE was a multicenter, open-label, parallel-group randomized controlled trial at 2 German university hospitals. Adults with early (stage I-III) breast cancer initiating systemic therapy were randomized 1:1 to reactive patient-reported outcome assessment (RPA) or control. Both arms received the ENABLE app with educational and organizational support and scheduled HRQoL assessments at 6 fixed time points; only RPA received weekly EuroQol Visual Analogue Scale screening (trigger: score <50 or ≥10-point decline) followed by symptom assessment, digital triage, and care-team alerts. Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System-29 was analyzed as an 8-measure HRQoL end-point family (7 domains plus pain intensity); no single domain, composite score, or binary global success rule was prespecified. Group-by-visit mixed-effects models were fitted with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate adjustment. The recruitment period was March 22, 2021, to September 8, 2023. Of 605 randomized patients, 487 entered the modified intention-to-treat analysis (RPA: n=242; control: n=245). End-of-treatment between-group differences (RPA minus control, T-score points, 95% CI, and adjusted P) were: fatigue -3.90 (95% CI -5.77 to -2.03; P=.004), social participation +2.84 (95% CI 1.18 to 4.49; P=.01), anxiety -2.10 (95% CI -3.65 to -0.55; P=.049), depression -1.95 (95% CI -3.25 to -0.65; P=.10), sleep disturbance -1.82 (95% CI -3.43 to -0.20; P=.051), pain interference -1.44 (95% CI -3.38 to 0.49; P=.18), physical function +1.33 (95% CI -0.22 to 2.88; P=.18), and pain intensity -0.26 (95% CI -0.73 to 0.21; P=.32; 0-10 scale). All T-score differences were below the 5-point minimally important difference (MID). Exploratory time-to-deterioration analyses favored RPA for fatigue (hazard ratio [HR] 0.69, 95% CI 0.54-0.89), social participation (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.59-0.97), and depression (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.44-0.98). Of 209 monitored RPA patients, 160 (76.6%; 95% CI 70.4-81.8) triggered at least 1 alert. No intervention-related harms were identified. ENABLE tests real-time, rule-based ePRO triage with care-team escalation against an active digital comparator rather than usual care, isolating the response pathway itself; it extends this design from metastatic disease into early breast cancer and escalates to the care team rather than to the patient alone. Benefits were domain-specific and sub-MID, in anxiety, fatigue, and social participation, tempering the expectation of a global HRQoL effect. For practice, symptom-triggered triage is a supportive-care workflow tool worth embedding where alerts reach a team that acts and documents, not a stand-alone remedy for treatment-related morbidity.

papers.title: Accelerometry-Based and Gyroscope-Based Detection of Sleep Apnea Events: Systematic Review of Technical and Clinical Evidence.
papers.abstract: Sleep apnea is a common but frequently underdiagnosed disorder associated with increased cardiovascular and metabolic risk. Although polysomnography remains the diagnostic gold standard, its high cost, technical complexity, and limited availability restrict large-scale screening and continuous monitoring. Accelerometry-based and gyroscope-based approaches may represent a simplified alternative that can also be applied in home-based settings. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the technical and clinical evidence for accelerometry-based and gyroscope-based detection of apnea and hypopnea events and to assess their potential clinical applicability. A systematic literature search was conducted on April 12, 2025, in PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines. Studies investigating accelerometers, gyroscopes, inertial measurement units, seismocardiography, or ballistocardiography for apnea or hypopnea detection were included. Extracted data comprised study characteristics, sensor configurations, signal processing approaches, validation strategies, diagnostic performance, and clinical applicability. Methodological quality was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. A total of 46 studies published between 2010 and 2025 were included. Most studies used accelerometers as the primary sensing modality, whereas gyroscopes were mainly applied in multimodal inertial measurement unit systems. Binary classification between apnea and nonapnea phases was the predominant analytical approach. Reported sensitivities ranged from 30% to 99%, depending on study settings, validation strategies, and evaluation levels. High diagnostic performance was mainly observed in simulation-based studies under controlled conditions. The included studies differed considerably in sensor placement, sampling frequencies, preprocessing pipelines, segmentation strategies, validation procedures, and reference standards. Only a minority of studies used polysomnography as the reference standard or included clinically representative populations. Furthermore, limited external validation, insufficient reproducibility, and a high risk of bias reduced comparability and clinical transferability. Current evidence supports the feasibility of accelerometer-based respiratory monitoring for sleep apnea screening, particularly in wearable and home-monitoring settings. However, most available studies were conducted under controlled experimental conditions and included only limited clinical validation. Standardized validation procedures and clinically representative cohorts are necessary to improve comparability and clinical transferability.

papers.title: Interactions between sleep parameters and heart rate variability in temporomandibular disorders.
papers.abstract: Temporomandibular disorders (TMD) cause pain and dysfunction in the temporomandibular joints (TMJs) and masticatory muscles and significantly impact quality of life. Temporomandibular disorderrelated pain is associated with sleep disorders and affects heart rate (HR) parameters; however, data from polysomnographic studies remains inconclusive. The aim of the study was to evaluate the impact of TMD on sleep parameters recorded using video-polysomnography (vPSG) and heart rate variability (HRV) monitored with the use of a 24-hour electrocardiogram (ECG). A cross-sectional study included 93 patients with TMD diagnosed according to the Diagnostic Criteria for Temporomandibular Disorders (DC/TMD). Video-polysomnography and 24-hour ECG monitoring were conducted. Pain was assessed using the numeric rating scale (NRS) (0-10) and categorized as mild (≤5) or severe (>5). The study included 93 patients with TMD, divided into groups of low pain intensity (n = 66) and high pain intensity (n = 27). The group with high pain intensity demonstrated lower sleep efficiency (87.7% vs. 90.8%, p = 0.022) and lower oxygen saturation (94.7% vs. 95.2%, p = 0.036). Heart rate variability parameters were similar in both groups. Women reported a higher total pain score (20 vs. 10, p = 0.007) and had a higher percentage of normal-to-normal (NN) intervals differing by more than 50 ms (pNN50) (24 h: 22.5% vs. 14.2%, p = 0.013; daytime: 18.0% vs. 9.8%, p = 0.002), higher daytime root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) (41.7 vs. 34.8, p = 0.026), and a higher nighttime HR (63.8 vs. 60.5, p = 0.047). Additionally, women demonstrated lower values for very low frequency (VLF) power (1,402.4 vs. 2,214.5, p = 0.010), low frequency (LF) power (1,415.5 vs. 2,494.5, p = 0.028), and the low frequency/high frequency (LF/HF) ratio (1.3 vs. 2.5, p < 0.001). High TMD-related pain intensity is associated with reduced sleep efficiency and lower mean oxygen saturation during sleep. Women experience higher pain intensity but lower sympathetic activation than men.

papers.title: Brain-computer interface technology for chronic pain management.
papers.abstract: Chronic pain remains inadequately managed by pharmacological and interventional therapies, which carry risks including opioid-related complications and limited long-term efficacy. Brain-computer interfaces (BCI) have emerged as a non-pharmacological therapeutic approach, most commonly implemented using noninvasive modalities such as scalp EEG or fMRI, that aims to target neural activity patterns associated with chronic pain. This review examines the principles underlying BCI systems and their application in chronic pain, including EEG-based neurofeedback targeting oscillatory activity, infraslow-frequency neurofeedback, a theta-controlled vibrotactile BCI, real-time fMRI-based neurofeedback, and emerging closed-loop neuromodulation systems. Advantages, limitations, and future directions are discussed. BCI technology represents a promising, but still early-stage, approach for chronic pain management. Clinical translation will depend less on decoding accuracy than on addressing regulatory and reimbursement barriers, conducting adequately powered, sham-controlled trials, and implementing patient stratification. Convergence with artificial intelligence and closed-loop neuromodulation is promising, but algorithmic sophistication should not be equated with clinical applicability. Wearable platforms raise data privacy and transparency concerns. BCIs are likely to be adjuncts within multimodal pain management, not replacements for existing treatments. Preliminary evidence supports feasibility, but adequately powered, sham-controlled trials are needed to establish treatment-specific and durable efficacy.

papers.title: Nocturnal Symptom Relief May Not Consistently Translate Into Measurable Sleep Improvement With Potassium-Competitive Acid Blocker Therapy.
Feasibility of Longitudinal Home Monitoring of Nocturnal Transcutaneous CO2 and Relationship to Standard Respiratory Measures in Patients With ALS: A Pilot Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) results in respiratory muscle weakness causing hypoventilation, retention of carbon dioxide (CO2), and chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure. In this pilot study, we performed a 12-month assessment of daytime and home nocturnal CO2 to track respiratory progression, determine relationships with surrogate respiratory measures, and assess the impact of non-invasive ventilatory support. Adults with forced vital capacity (FVC) less than 90% predicted secondary to ALS were recruited from two sites in the northeast US. Participants were followed up at standard visits every 3 months for up to five visits. Spirometry, functional scores, and patient-reported outcomes of dyspnea were recorded. Each visit included a 15-min, seated measurement of transcutaneous CO2 (PtcCO2) while in clinic, followed by 3 nights of home overnight PtcCO2 monitoring. Linear mixed-effects models were employed to describe the changes that occurred longitudinally and resulting from the initiation of non-invasive ventilation (NIV). Sixteen subjects were enrolled, with nine completing the full study. Strength and FVC declined over time, while daytime PtcCO2 remained stable. Five individuals demonstrated nocturnal hypercapnia that preceded FVC < 50% predicted normal. Transition to NIV was associated with a 7 mmHg decrease in nocturnal PtcCO2. Home nocturnal PtcCO2 assessment in ALS may identify respiratory insufficiency prior to FVC. Transcutaneous CO2 may play a role in the respiratory management of patients as a biomarker for hypoventilation risk and NIV titration. However, equipment availability and data quality limitations would benefit from professional assistance rather than independent in-home use.

papers.title: Peripheral sensory neurons clock genes are a molecular driver of pain rhythmicity.
papers.abstract: Pain intensity fluctuates across the day in patients, yet the cellular clock mechanisms that generate pain rhythmicity and their therapeutic potential remain poorly defined. Prior studies have established circadian variation in nociception and a requirement for intact clock function, but it has remained unclear the neurophysiological mechanisms which translate clock state into time-of-day changes in pain. The goal of this study was to define the clock component(s) and effector pathway(s) that drive pain rhythmicity and to test whether this axis can be exploited for analgesia. We combined behavioural analyses under circadian conditions with genetic dissection of clock components in sensory neurons, electrophysiological interrogation of nociceptor excitability, and pharmacological modulation of the clock machinery. To establish translational relevance, we used human iPSC-derived nociceptors, including a human pain disease model, to test whether the same clock-excitability coupling operates in human cells. We show that nociceptive behaviours exhibit robust circadian rhythmicity and that this rhythmicity depends on the molecular clock within peripheral sensory neurons. Loss of cryptochromes CRY1/CRY2 disrupts time-of-day differences in nociceptor excitability, identifying cryptochromes as essential clock effectors in the pain pathway. Mechanistically, cryptochrome state controls voltage-gated sodium channel function, providing a direct link from clock machinery to nociceptor responsiveness. Pharmacological stabilisation of cryptochromes using a small-molecule modulator suppresses sodium currents and reduces nociceptive responses across distinct pain paradigms, and this effect is abrogated when cryptochrome function is absent. In synchronised human iPSC-derived nociceptors, we observe concordant clock-state-dependent changes in excitability, and cryptochrome stabilisation reduces hyperexcitability. These findings identify a peripheral sensory neuron clock mechanism that drives pain rhythmicity through cryptochrome-dependent control of sodium channel function and highlight cryptochrome stabilisation as a non-opioid therapeutic strategy for pain disorders with diurnal symptom variation.

papers.title: Linking Attainment of Wearable-Derived Sleep and Physical Activity Recommendations with Cardiometabolic Biomarkers and Employer Health Care Claims: A Feasibility Study.
papers.abstract: Among 80 wearable members stratified into quartiles of attainment of combined physical-activity and sleep recommendations, higher attainment showed age-adjusted associations with lower resting heart rate and BMI and higher heart rate variability. The lowest-attainment quartile incurred approximately 12-fold higher annual per-member health care spending than the other quartiles.

papers.title: A generative framework for estimating brain energy landscapes from continuous neuroimaging observations.
papers.abstract: Pairwise maximum entropy models (pMEMs) are gaining increasing attention as a principled way to study nonlinear brain-state transitions. By representing each brain region as a binary active/inactive state and estimating the least-biased probability distribution over all such network configurations, pMEMs reconstruct an energy landscape in which local minima correspond to stable or metastable brain states and transitions reflect movement across attractor basins. However, neuroimaging recordings are continuous and spatially mixed, forcing conventional pMEM analyses to demean and hard-threshold each channel. This ad hoc binarization discards amplitude information and can conflate spatially correlated noise or source mixing with genuine neural coupling. We introduce a hierarchical generative pMEM that links latent binary network states to continuous observations. Node-specific baseline and gain parameters model amplitude modulation, compound-symmetry noise captures shared residual covariance, and, for electroencephalography/magnetoencephalography (EEG/MEG), the electromagnetic leadfield is included as a generative forward model rather than a preprocessing inverse. Model parameters and latent states are jointly estimated using exact posterior enumeration for the small networks analyzed here and a mean-field extension for larger networks. Controlled simulations demonstrated two complementary advantages of the proposed framework. Residual-covariance modeling improved recovery of pMEM fields, couplings, and latent states by accounting for shared fluctuations, with the clearest gains when residual spatial correlation was sufficiently strong. The generative leadfield model further improved sensor-space inference by avoiding inverse-first source reconstruction, including settings in which covariance modeling alone offered limited gains. Resting-state EEG validation showed higher residual correlation during eyes-closed than eyes-open rest, consistent with elevated and spatially coherent alpha activity. Applied further to propofol sedation EEG (alpha-band amplitude envelopes, 8-13 Hz), the fitted 6-node default mode network (DMN) model showed pipeline-dependent condition effects in residual spatial correlation and basin entropy, not apparent under the conventional demean-based pMEM.

papers.title: Unequal Burden: Sex Differences in Cannabis Withdrawal Symptom Severity in People With Multiple Sclerosis-A Short Report.
papers.abstract: People with multiple sclerosis (MS) frequently use cannabis to manage symptoms such as pain, spasticity, and sleep disturbance. During abstinence, withdrawal symptoms may overlap with MS-related complaints, complicating cessation. This study examined whether cannabis withdrawal trajectories differ by sex during monitored abstinence in people with MS. Nineteen frequent cannabis users with MS (11 women) completed 28 days of monitored abstinence. Withdrawal symptoms were assessed using the Cannabis Withdrawal Questionnaire (CWQ) at baseline and weekly through day 28. Abstinence was verified using creatinine-adjusted urinary THC-COOH ratios. Mood was assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) at baseline and day 28. A repeated-measures analysis of covariance examined time × sex effects, adjusting for demographic, disability, and cannabis-use covariates. At baseline (preabstinence), women reported higher CWQ scores than men. On day 28, women again showed higher scores. A significant time × sex interaction (Pillai trace = .784; P = .018; partial η² = .784) indicated distinct symptom trajectories across abstinence. Women reported greater irritability, sleep disturbance, physical tension, nausea, and headaches. HADS scores remained stable and within normal limits for both sexes. Women with MS demonstrated a more pronounced and sustained increase in CWQ symptom burden over the abstinence period than men. These findings likely reflect both withdrawal-related effects and the unmasking of underlying MS-related symptoms. Cannabis cessation appears psychologically tolerable in people with MS, though women may require closer monitoring and targeted support during abstinence.

papers.title: Who's Been Sleeping in My Bedroom? Associations Between Co-Sleeping with Dogs, Cats, or Children and Sleep and Cardiorespiratory Physiology Among WHOOP Users.
papers.abstract: Co-sleeping with pets or children is common, yet its associations with sleep, cardiorespiratory physiology, and behavioral outcomes are understudied. We examined within-person associations between co-sleeping with a dog, cat, or child and sleep characteristics, measures of cardiorespiratory physiology, and next-day physical activity. We analyzed 1,649,083 person-days from 11,733 adults wearing the WHOOP wearable device. Participants self-reported nightly co-sleeping via a daily journal in the device's companion smartphone application. Linear mixed-effects models compared nights with and without co-sleeping within the same individual. Co-sleeping was associated with lower resting heart rate (0.8-1.1 beats/min), lower respiratory rate (0.04-0.07 breaths/min), and higher heart rate variability (1.41-1.95 ms). Sleep outcomes were mixed, with longer sleep duration (5.5-9.6 min) but more disturbances (0.36-0.40 instances) and slightly less restorative sleep (0.23-1.17%). Associations were generally consistent across groups, although child co-sleeping was associated with greater sleep disruption. Next-day physical activity was higher following dog and cat co-sleeping (7.6 and 7.4 intensity-weighted min, respectively) but lower following child co-sleeping (-2.6 intensity-weighted min). Despite statistical significance, all standardized effect sizes were small (β range: 0.008-0.045). Co-sleeping was associated with small differences in cardiorespiratory physiology (lower resting heart rate, higher heart rate variability) alongside mildly greater sleep disruption. The small magnitude of these associations suggests that co-sleeping decisions may be influenced more by personal and contextual factors than by expectations of substantive physiologic or sleep-related impacts.

papers.title: Generalized myoclonus following dobutamine stress echocardiography: a case report.
papers.abstract: Dobutamine stress echocardiography (DSE) is a widely used and generally safe non-invasive imaging modality for the assessment of myocardial ischaemia. Adverse effects are predominantly cardiovascular, whereas neurological complications are exceedingly rare. Dobutamine-induced myoclonus (DIM) has only rarely been reported, mainly in patients receiving prolonged dobutamine infusions for heart failure or cardiomyopathy. A 47-year-old woman underwent DSE for evaluation of exertional chest pain. Following completion of a standard dobutamine protocol, she developed generalized rhythmic myoclonic jerks predominantly involving the axial musculature. The patient remained fully conscious and hemodynamically stable throughout the episode. Intravenous diazepam failed to improve symptoms, whereas complete resolution occurred after administration of intravenous valproic acid. Laboratory investigations, including electrolytes, renal function, and thyroid function tests, were normal. Electroencephalography and brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed no abnormalities. No recurrence was observed during hospitalization or follow-up. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of DIM occurring immediately after DSE. Unlike previously published cases, which predominantly involved patients with chronic kidney disease and developed after prolonged dobutamine exposure, our patient had normal renal function and developed symptoms immediately upon completion of the stress protocol. The pathophysiology remains uncertain, although increased central nervous system exposure to dobutamine has been proposed. Clinicians performing DSE should be aware of myoclonus as a rare but important neurological complication and should consider valproic acid when benzodiazepines fail to achieve symptom control.

papers.title: The role and mechanism of endothelial cell-specific molecule-1 in respiratory diseases.
papers.abstract: Endothelial cell-specific molecule-1 (ESM1) is a soluble dermatan sulfate proteoglycan and is mainly expressed in pulmonary endothelial cells. It is reported that ESM1 plays an important role in promoting cell proliferation, such as metabolic reprogramming, and inhibiting autophagy. In addition, ESM1 exerts a dual regulatory effect on inflammation. However, the mechanism of the dual regulatory effect of ESM1 on inflammation remains unclear. Moreover, evidence suggests that ESM1 is involved in multiple signaling pathways, such as the EGFR/ESM1, EGFR/HER3-Akt/ANGPT2, HGF/c-MET, VEGF-A/ESM1, mTOR, and ZEB1/PI3K/AKT pathways. Increasing studies suggested that ESM1 is involved in various respiratory diseases, such as lung cancer, obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS), pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), and acute lung injury (ALI)/acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). In lung cancer, ESM1 promotes cancer cell proliferation through the EGFR, NF-κB, and HGF/c-MET signaling pathways. In OSAHS, ESM1 enhances inflammatory factor secretion and monocyte-endothelial cell adhesion through the HIF-1α/VEGF signaling pathway. In PAH, ESM1 may promote vascular remodeling and inflammation via a positive feedback loop with TNF-α. Conversely, in ALI/ARDS, ESM1 may inhibit leukocyte recruitment to reduce inflammation. However, the specific roles and mechanisms of ESM1 in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, and pneumonia need to be further explored. Accordingly, ESM1 may serve as a potential therapeutic target for various respiratory diseases.

papers.title: Neurologist-focused workflows for immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome in CAR T-cell therapy and CD3-engaging bispecific antibodies.
papers.abstract: To synthesize current evidence into a neurologist-focused workflow for early recognition, bedside monitoring, diagnostic triage, mitigation, and therapy-specific surveillance of immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar were searched in English from inception through 25 March 2026. Of 201 records, 18 duplicates were removed, 183 were screened, 157 full texts were assessed, and 26 studies were included in a narrative synthesis. The selection process was reported using applicable PRISMA 2020 elements and the narrative presentation was evaluated using SANRA. Evidence supports early neurologic co-management in selected high-risk patients, serial language- and attention-sensitive bedside assessment, and clinically triggered rather than routine electroencephalography. Pilot neurocognitive data suggest that subtle decline may precede deterioration on the Immune Effector Cell-Associated Encephalopathy (ICE) score. Bispecific-antibody programs generally show lower neurotoxicity burdens than many CAR T-cell platforms but create repeated risk windows around step-up dosing and outpatient transition. Delayed B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-associated movement and neurocognitive syndromes remain an important safety signal, although therapeutic evidence is largely observational or case based. The evidence supports documenting a baseline neurologic phenotype, performing serial bedside monitoring, deploying electroencephalography and neuroimaging when results may change management, and maintaining product-specific vigilance for delayed syndromes. Tiered pathways are needed for community and resource-limited settings.

papers.title: When a Seizure Reveals More Than a Hemorrhage: When to Suspect Cerebral Cavernous Malformations.
papers.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are low-flow vascular malformations that may be asymptomatic or present with seizures, hemorrhage, headache, or focal neurological deficits. Most are sporadic and solitary, whereas familial CCMs are associated with multiple lesions and autosomal-dominant inheritance. Distinguishing between these forms is clinically relevant for long-term management. We present a 33-year-old woman who presented with generalized tonic-clonic seizures following sleep deprivation. Computed tomography (CT) initially suggested a left frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) subsequently revealed two left frontal Zabramski type II CCMs. Electroencephalography showed cortical dysfunction with paroxysmal activity and contralateral propagation. Antiseizure treatment with phenytoin was initiated and later supplemented with levetiracetam. The patient remained asymptomatic and was referred for tertiary evaluation. This case highlights the diagnostic limitations of CT and the importance of MRI for CCM characterization and detection of multiple lesions. The presence of two cavernomas and a potentially relevant family history raises suspicion for familial CCM, although these findings alone do not establish a hereditary diagnosis. Genetic evaluation and detailed family assessment should therefore be considered. Treatment should be individualized; conservative management is appropriate in selected stable patients, whereas microsurgery and stereotactic radiosurgery are reserved for specific clinical scenarios.

papers.title: Development and validation of a low-cost, wearable near-infrared spectroscopy system for quantifying tissue water fraction in the human brain.
papers.abstract: Cerebral water fraction is physiologically relevant to brain fluid dynamics, glymphatic function, cerebral edema, and dehydration, yet it is not routinely measured in wearable neuroimaging. We aimed to develop and validate a low-cost, wearable, light-emitting diode (LED)-based continuous-wave near-infrared spectroscopy system capable of concurrently monitoring changes in cerebral hemoglobin concentration and water fraction from the forehead. Our device, called the GS-FlexNIRS, contains nine LEDs spanning 740 to 1050 nm mounted on a flexible printed circuit board. Three of these wavelengths (i.e., 910, 940, and 1050 nm) fall within the water absorption window. A wavelength-weighted fitting algorithm incorporates measured LED emission spectra and photodiode responsivity to enable accurate chromophore recovery despite spectrally broad LED illumination. Performance was characterized in liquid phantoms and in five healthy participants during respiratory maneuvers. The system achieved a dynamic range of ∼ 100 dB , gain linearity ( R 2 > 0.99997 ), and signal-to-noise ratio of 67 to 90 dB. Phantom experiments confirmed independent tracking of hemoglobin deoxygenation and water fraction changes. Hemoglobin responses in human measurements were consistent with prior work. The GS-FlexNIRS ( ∼ $ 350 / unit ) and its wearable design may support future longitudinal and naturalistic monitoring of cerebral hemodynamics and brain fluid dynamics, enabling investigation in sleep, glymphatic research, and cerebral edema monitoring.

papers.title: Preliminary Evidence Suggests the Transcriptomic Response of Tricolored Bats to White-Nose Syndrome Is Similar but Not Identical to That of Little Brown Bats.
papers.abstract: Understanding the pathophysiology of emerging wildlife diseases can inform treatment, improve the projections of long-term population trajectories, and reveal variation in population-level impacts among species. Research on white-nose syndrome (WNS) in hibernating North American bats has largely focused on a single highly susceptible species, the little brown bat (Myotis lucifugus). Another susceptible species, the tricolored bat (Perimyotis subflavus), has experienced population declines comparable to or greater than those of little brown bats but remains understudied. In particular, the immune response of tricolored bats to WNS has not previously been evaluated. Here, we conduct a preliminary analysis comparing part of the transcriptomic response of tricolored bats to WNS with the little brown bat response. We analyzed 14 tricolored and 13 little brown bat samples collected from Colossal Cave, Kentucky, USA in 2017, where WNS has been present since 2013. We also included 26 little brown bat samples collected from a nearby hibernation site in 1999, prior to WNS emergence. Lacking a proper pre-WNS control for tricolored bats, we conducted pairwise differential expression analyses between the three sample groups and evaluated the overlap between results to infer part of the tricolored bat response to WNS. These initial results suggested that tricolored bats exhibited differential expression patterns characteristic of susceptible species, including large changes in gene expression still apparent at the end of the hibernation season. Differentially expressed genes were associated with immune, metabolic, and circadian functions, broadly resembling the response observed in little brown bats. However, there was variation in the specific genes involved between the two species. Overall, tricolored bats appear to mount a pronounced immune response to WNS that is similar, but not identical, to that of little brown bats.

papers.title: Cryptococcal meningitis-associated cerebrovascular injury presenting with sequential multifocal cerebral infarctions and prominent autonomic dysfunction in a non-HIV patient: a case report and focused literature review.
papers.abstract: Cryptococcal meningitis (CM) can occur in patients without human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and may be complicated by genuine cerebral infarction, creating a powerful diagnostic anchor toward primary cerebrovascular disease. We report a 66-year-old non-HIV man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and no documented major immunosuppressive condition who initially presented with dizziness and mild headache. Brain MRI showed restricted diffusion in the left brainstem, and acute ischemic stroke was diagnosed. Over the following weeks, neurological deterioration continued despite stroke-directed treatment. Repeat MRI demonstrated new infarctions involving the left cerebellar vermis, corpus callosum, and left thalamus, while the patient developed rapid cognitive decline and prominent autonomic manifestations, including orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, constipation, vomiting, and severe sleep disturbance. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination revealed an opening pressure >300 mmH2O, leukocytes 128 × 106/L, protein 964 mg/L, and glucose 1.28 mmol/L. India ink staining was suspiciously positive, and Cryptococcus neoformans was confirmed by fungal culture and metagenomic next-generation sequencing. Serial lumbar punctures and antifungal treatment with amphotericin B and fluconazole were followed by substantial clinical improvement. To contextualize the case, we conducted a focused review of published non-HIV or apparently immunocompetent reports of CM-associated cerebral infarction. The literature shows a recurring pattern of deep perforator, brainstem, cerebellar, callosal, and multifocal ischemic injury, with both small- and large-vessel mechanisms reported. However, sequential infarctions across multiple territories accompanied by a prominent progressive autonomic syndrome remain poorly documented. This case supports early CSF investigation when recurrent infarction, encephalopathic progression, and multisystem neurological features are discordant with an isolated vascular diagnosis.

papers.title: Diphenhydramine disrupts sleep architecture in 5XFAD Alzheimer's disease model and wild-type mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption is common in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Diphenhydramine (DPH), a first-generation antihistamine with anticholinergic properties, is widely used as an over-the-counter sleep aid. We tested whether chronic DPH treatment alters sleep architecture in 5XFAD and wild-type female mice. Female 5XFAD (n = 16) and wild-type (WT) littermates (n = 14) were implanted with wireless telemetry recording devices to measure electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) continuously. After a 24h baseline recording at 5 months of age, mice received oral DPH (10 mg/kg) or vehicle at ZT0 for one month. After this chronic treatment, sleep was recorded continuously for 48h during ongoing dosing. Sleep was scored as rapid eye movement (REM), non-rapid eye movement (NREM) 1, NREM2, or wake. A survival curve analysis was used to investigate the microarchitecture of sleep phases after chronic diphenhydramine treatment. At baseline, 5XFAD female mice had more time in NREM1 than WT female controls and had shorter REM and NREM2 bouts. Chronic DPH treatment fragmented NREM2 in both genotypes, reducing long NREM2 bouts. DPH increased total duration of NREM1 and REM during the active phase, and disrupted the light-dark distribution of sleep. DPH did not rescue 5XFAD sleep deficits; instead, DPH treatment resulted in NREM2 fragmentation. Overall, chronic DPH use degrades sleep quality and increases fragmentation in both WT and AD-model female mice, which questions the use of sedating anticholinergics as sleep aids, especially in AD.
papers.journal: Neurobiology of sleep and circadian rhythms

papers.title: A Physiological Optics Characterization of the Bagolini bar for Testing Density of Suppression.
papers.abstract: To characterize the spectral and photometric properties of the 16 filters of a commercial Bagolini bar and to determine whether successive filter numbers correspond to a uniform progression of spectral attenuation, illuminance, and interocular contrast. An instrumental spectrophotometric characterization of the 16 filters of a commercial Bagolini bar was performed. Spectral measurements were acquired over the 320-810 nm instrumental range, with the 380-780 nm visible range used for the principal spectral analysis. Spectrophotometric analysis demonstrated non-linear, step-wise changes in the optical properties of successive Bagolini filters. The transmission spectrum peak with increasing filter number shifted from approximately 610 nm to 770 nm. The transmitted light intensity and Weber contrast also exhibited non-uniform, step-wise changes. The 16 filters do not provide a uniformly graded progression of optical attenuation. The measured spectral and photometric transitions provide an optical basis for testable hypotheses concerning non-uniform perceptual responses, but their clinical consequences require psychophysical and clinical validation.

papers.title: Home Sleep Apnea Testing Over 25 Years: A Bibliometric Analysis of Global Research Trends.
papers.abstract: Home sleep apnea tests (HSATs) have emerged as alternatives for diagnosing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). We conducted a 25-year bibliometric analysis to characterize international research trends in Type 3 and 4 HSATs, focusing on publication, authorship, country of origin, HSAT type, and study design. MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Embase were searched for studies published from January 2000 to December 2025. Publications primarily evaluating Type 3 or 4 HSATs for OSA diagnosis in children or adults were included. Linear regression and Cochran-Armitage trend tests were used to assess temporal trends. The literature search yielded 6755 articles, with 487 articles included in the final analysis. From 2020 to 2025, the top five journals of publication were respiratory and sleep-related journals. Publication output increased significantly over time, at a rate of 1.127 articles per year (p < 0.001). From 2020 to 2025, the five most common journals were respiratory or sleep-related. The United States accounted for the largest proportion of publications (33.3%), followed by China and Canada. The proportion of authors with medical degrees increased by 1.08% annually (p = 0.042), while PhD and MD/PhD authorship remained stable. The number of institutions and departments represented among authors also remained stable (p = 0.248 and p = 0.323, respectively). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first bibliometric analysis of research trends in Type 3 and 4 HSATs. HSAT research has expanded substantially over the past 25 years, with increasing publication output and multi-authorship. Diagnostic cohort studies have consistently dominated the literature, while recent growth in secondary research suggests increasing maturity of the field and capacity for evidence synthesis. Rising MD authorship alongside stable PhD and MD/PhD representation suggests increasing clinician involvement. The United States remains the leading contributor, potentially reflecting greater access to research funding and resources.

papers.title: A representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion framework for spectral analysis and detection of epileptiform patterns in pediatric EEG: computational validation with a roadmap for external benchmarking.
papers.abstract: Pediatric EEG analysis for epilepsy detection is challenged by the non-stationary and developmentally heterogeneous nature of epileptiform activity. Conventional Fourier approaches provide limited time-frequency localization, whereas single-domain methods such as the wavelet transform and empirical mode decomposition (EMD) each exhibit complementary weaknesses. We developed a representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion framework that integrates wavelet and EMD spectra before feature extraction. The pipeline included adaptive wavelet denoising, energy-criterion EMD, weighted time-frequency fusion, extraction of eight spectral-temporal features, and classification using a soft-voting ensemble of a radial basis function support vector machine, random forest, and neural network. Evaluation was performed on 2,000 synthetic pediatric EEG segments spanning canonical epileptiform morphologies and multiple signal-to-noise ratios. A feature-level fusion variant was implemented as an ablation comparator to isolate the effect of fusion strategy while preserving identical feature extraction, classifier architecture, and validation procedures. Across 10-fold stratified cross-validation with 100 Monte Carlo replications, the proposed framework achieved 94.6 ± 0.6% accuracy, 93.7 ± 0.8% sensitivity, 95.5 ± 0.5% specificity, F1 score of 0.943 ± 0.007, and AUROC of 0.971 (95% CI, 0.962-0.978). Performance exceeded standalone wavelet, EMD, and Fourier baselines (all p < 0.001). Representation-level fusion also outperformed feature-level fusion by 1.4 percentage points in accuracy, with the greatest gains observed for polyspike and slow-wave morphologies. On the synthetic corpus the framework was competitive with EEGNet and a 1D convolutional network while retaining explicit time-frequency interpretability. In an external feasibility validation on the CHB-MIT pediatric scalp EEG corpus (14 subjects, leave-one-subject-out), representation-level fusion attained the highest performance of all methods (AUROC 0.901, accuracy 86.7%), confirming that the fusion strategy transfers to real recordings, with performance decreasing as expected. Representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion provides an interpretable and transparent computational framework for analyzing non-stationary pediatric epileptiform EEG whose advantage over classical time-frequency baselines persists, at feasibility scale, on real CHB-MIT recordings and remains competitive with deep-learning baselines. Because the primary evaluation is synthetic and the external validation is a feasibility-scale demonstration, these figures should be read as evidence of methodological viability and external transportability rather than definitive clinical performance; validation on larger, multi-center and prospective pediatric cohorts is the essential next step.

papers.title: Lights Out in the Canopy: Arboreal Camera Traps Offer New Insights Into Sleeping-Site Partitioning and Sleep Ecology in Primate Communities.
papers.abstract: Sleep is an essential yet costly biological process, leaving animals vulnerable to predation and constraining their use of space and time. Optimal sleeping sites therefore represent valuable, potentially contested resources, yet they remain largely overlooked in primate community ecology. Understanding how syntopic species compete for and partition sleeping sites can reveal mechanisms of coexistence, but community-level studies remain limited because multiple arboreal species are difficult to monitor simultaneously. Here, we used arboreal camera traps to investigate sleeping-site use and spatiotemporal partitioning within a Brazilian Atlantic Forest primate community. Over 7 months (2024-2025), we monitored ten Copaifera trapezifolia trees used as preferred sleeping sites by southern muriquis (Brachyteles arachnoides), brown howler monkeys (Alouatta guariba) and black-tufted capuchins (Sapajus nigritus cucullatus), recording 4195 videos documenting 1253 visits and 158 sleeping nights. C. trapezifolia trees constituted a shared but limited resource, and access reflected predicted interspecific differences in resource holding potential (RHP), the relative ability of a species to prevail in direct contests over a shared resource. Muriquis and capuchins, the higher-RHP species with larger home ranges, showed high temporal overlap in copaíba use-preferentially sleeping there on warmer nights and under lower lunar illumination, suggesting roles for thermoregulation and perceived predation risk-offset by reduced spatial overlap, consistent with greater ranging flexibility enabling spatial avoidance. Howlers, constrained by more restricted ranging and repeatedly displaced in direct encounters with the other species, instead relied on temporal segregation to access the same preferred trees. Nocturnal videos further revealed activity beyond residual wakefulness at the edges of the night, offering rare direct evidence of nocturnal behaviour and fragmented sleep in wild arboreal primates. These findings indicate that sleeping sites can function as contested, high-value resources structuring primate community dynamics through asymmetric contest competition, and highlight arboreal camera trapping as a powerful tool for studying primate sleep ecology.

papers.title: Effects of chronic alcohol consumption on gene expression in the rat left ventricle: a transcriptomic analysis.
papers.abstract: Chronic alcohol consumption is one of the leading causes of dilated cardiomyopathy. Alcohol-associated cardiomyopathy (ACM) is characterized by impaired cardiac function and ventricular dilation in individuals with a history of long-term alcohol consumption. Alcohol exerts adverse effects on the myocardium via mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic inflammation. However, the broader transcriptional changes associated with chronic alcohol exposure remain poorly understood. A chronic ethanol feeding model was utilized, in which male Wistar rats were fed a Lieber-Decarli ethanol diet containing 6.7% (v/v) ethanol (ET) or an isocaloric control (CONT) diet for 6 weeks. Left ventricular tissues were collected from ET-fed and CONT-fed rats. Differential gene expression was assessed using bulk RNA sequencing, followed by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA). Transcriptomic analysis identified 194 upregulated and 199 downregulated genes in the left ventricles of ET-fed rats compared with CONT-fed rats. IPA revealed downregulated pathways related to the circadian clock and interferon signaling in the myocardium of ET-fed rats. In particular, the differentially altered genes included regulators of the circadian clock (Bmal1, Npas2, Per1, Per2) and interferon signaling (Ifit2, Ifit3, Irf6, Irf9). In contrast, pathways associated with mitochondrial RNA degradation, sheddase signaling, and neutrophil extracellular traps were upregulated in the myocardium following chronic ethanol exposure. Chronic ethanol exposure is associated with dysregulation of circadian rhythm and immune-related signaling pathways in the rat myocardium. These findings highlight molecular pathways that may contribute to the development of ACM and warrant further mechanistic investigation.

papers.title: Body mass index and health-related lifestyle behaviors among university students in Saudi Arabia: a single center cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Overweight and obesity are important public-health concerns among young adults. University students experience changes in dietary, physical-activity, sleep, and other health behaviors, but evidence from Saudi university populations remains heterogeneous. To explore associations between BMI and selected dietary, physical-activity, sleep, and sociodemographic characteristics among university students. This cross-sectional study analyzed electronic questionnaire responses collected from January to April 2025 on a sample of 196 students. Weight and height were self-reported and BMI was recalculated as weight (kg)/height2 (m2). BMI was categorized as underweight (<18.5), normal (18.5 to <24.9), overweight (25 to <30), or obesity (≥30 kg/m2). Associations were examined using contingency-table analyses and limited exploratory multivariable linear and logistic regression models. Among 196 analyzed students, 17 (8.7%) were underweight, 106 (54.1%) had normal BMI, 38 (19.4%) were overweight, and 35 (17.9%) had obesity; thus, 73 (37.2%) had overweight or obesity. Associations of BMI category with lifestyle were not statistically significant. Electronic-device use before bed showed a sparse-cell association (χ 2=23.438, df = 9, Monte Carlo p = 0.010) that should be considered exploratory. In adjusted linear regression, male sex (β = 5.26 kg/m2, 95% CI 2.36-8.16, p < 0.001), and students aged >23 years had higher BMI (β = 2.86, 95% CI 0.44-5.29, p = 0.021). In adjusted logistic regression, male sex (OR = 2.71, 95% CI 1.19-6.19, p = 0.018) and age >23 years (OR = 3.15, 95% CI 1.17-8.43, p = 0.023) were associated with overweight/obesity. Overweight and obesity were common. Gender and age showed associations with BMI status, whereas evidence for independent associations of the selected lifestyle measures was limited and imprecise. The cross-sectional design and self-reported measurements preclude causal inference.

papers.title: Beyond Static Representations: Learning Electroencephalogram Spatiotemporal Dynamics for Enhanced Emotion Recognition.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based emotion recognition plays a pivotal role in brain-computer interfaces and mental health monitoring. However, conventional approaches often neglect the intrinsic spatial correlations among EEG channels and fail to effectively model both global temporal dependencies and the continuity of neural oscillations. To overcome these challenges, we propose the Dynamic Spatial Embedding and Temporal Attention Mamba (DSE-TAM) framework. Our Dynamic Spatial Embedding (DSE) module leverages graph convolutional networks to dynamically capture inter-channel relationships, preserving spatial coherence in EEG representations. Subsequently, the Temporal Attention Mamba module integrates self-attention with state-space models to jointly optimize long-range temporal dependencies and smooth transition dynamics. Extensive experiments on 2 public benchmarks (DEAP and DREAMER) and an in-house CEED dataset demonstrate that DSE-TAM surpasses state-of-the-art methods, achieving accuracies of 79.75% (arousal) and 78.27% (valence) on DEAP, 80.55% (arousal) and 83.91% (valence) on DREAMER, and 73.75% (3-class) on CEED. These results validate the framework's efficacy in advancing EEG-based emotion decoding for brain-computer interfaces. The source code is available at https://github.com/Raizeroko/DSE-TAM.

papers.title: Advances in artificial intelligence for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis of neurological diseases: a systematic literature review.
papers.abstract: Brain imaging is central to the structural, functional, metabolic, and neurophysiological characterization of neurological disease, yet interpretation remains constrained by heterogeneity in acquisition, annotation, expertise, and clinical context. This systematic literature review evaluates recent artificial intelligence approaches for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis, with emphasis on methods, modalities, neurological diseases, diagnostic tasks, datasets, validation practices, and translational limitations. The review followed PRISMA 2020 and covered peer-reviewed English-language studies published from January 2020 through June 2026. Eight information sources were searched using database-specific terms for artificial intelligence, neuroimaging, neurological disease, and diagnostic analysis. The search identified 1,078 records; 236 duplicates were removed, 842 unique records were screened, 258 full texts were assessed, and 123 studies were included after a record-level eligibility re-audit. Heterogeneous evidence was synthesized narratively and by descriptive mapping rather than meta-analysis. MRI was frequently represented in the included studies and auxiliary mapping data; CT was commonly used in acute stroke and intracranial hemorrhage; PET supported selected molecular and differential-diagnosis studies; fMRI and diffusion imaging were used for network and white-matter analysis; and EEG extended the scope to neurophysiological diagnosis. CNN and three-dimensional networks were commonly reported, while attention, Transformer, graph, self-supervised, generative, multimodal, and foundation-model approaches appeared in selected recent studies. Stroke, dementia, and brain tumors were frequently represented, but heterogeneous populations, outcomes, and incomplete validation extraction precluded ranking diseases, modalities, architectures, or validation strategies. The evidence suggests movement from task-specific pattern recognition toward multimodal and context-rich decision support in selected settings, but it does not establish uniform methodological superiority or clinical maturity. Dependable translation requires patient-level data governance, transparent reporting, uncertainty estimation, independent multicenter testing, prospective workflow evaluation, and clinically meaningful endpoints.

papers.title: Federated Spiking GANs with Rényi Differential Privacy for privacy-preserving synthetic EEG generation in brain-computer interfaces.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) data used in brain-computer and brain-machine interfaces (BCI/BMI) contain sensitive, user-specific information, creating privacy risks in consumer applications such as gaming, human augmentation, and virtual reality. Existing methods like encryption and anonymization either fail to protect data during analysis or still expose identifiable attributes. While differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, it often reduces data utility. The key challenge is to generate synthetic EEG data that protects sensitive attributes while retaining temporal features for downstream use. To address this, we developed a federated spiking generative framework that integrates a spiking neural network (SNN)-based generator, temporally correlated noise, an artificial neural network (ANN)-based discriminator, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) within a federated learning framework. The SNN-based generator captures temporal characteristics, and the ANN-based discriminator maintains classification accuracy. Federated training prevents centralization of raw client data, while privacy is preserved through controlled perturbation of spike-train and membrane-potential representations, supported by RDP-based privacy accounting. We evaluated our architecture against methods such as RDP-TimeGAN, RDP-CRNN-GAN, RDP-RCGAN, and RDP-Clare-GAN, demonstrating that our approach preserves temporal features and downstream utility while maintaining privacy in synthetic EEG generation. This solution enables privacy-preserving generation of distributed synthetic EEG data for BCI/BMI research and development.

papers.title: Analysis of the potential profile and influencing factors of health behavior protection motivation in patients with unruptured intracranial aneurysms based on protection motivation theory.
papers.abstract: Rupture of unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIA) is the third leading cause of morbidity and mortality from cerebrovascular disease, with a disability rate as high as 36-58%; health behaviors are crucial for reducing the risk of rupture.
